Dedication


        This book is dedicated to my great-
       grandmother  Eleanor  Jane  Ashby
        Nielson, who died five days before my
          fifth birthday. I still vividly remember
       her immaculate garden of roses and
             I do not exaggerate when  I say that       flowers—a wonder in the desert.  I
      on many days, every single plate, cup,        honestly  thought  she was  magic.
       and bowl  in our house was being       Thank you  for teaching me to be
       used  to  make  botanical   paints,        fascinated by flowers.
        pigments, and dyes. So, if you enjoy
         this book, the person to thank is my
         wife, Charmayne. She allowed  this
       massive disruption to our kitchen FOR
        FIVE YEARS. The only complaint I ever
       heard from her was  in  frustration
       because she could not find a bowl for
        lunch:  “I think  I  will buy my own
       bowls and hide them from you.” We
      ended up buying dozens more bowls.
        This book is only possible because of
       her generosity of spirit. As I write this,
       she  is headed up the canyon, by
         herself,   to   get  me   a   single
        thimbleberry to test with a particular
       mordant to help me meet a deadline.
       She is very much looking forward to
        getting her kitchen back. Thank you
         for taking me on. This book  is also
        dedicated to you. I love you.

Why I Wrote This Book


Have you ever experienced the heartbreak of a beloved vessel or ceramic piece cracking or
breaking apart? Kintsugi is the art of beautifully mending broken pottery and prolonging its li
    Kintsugi is a traditional Japanese method of repairing ceramic using lacquers made from
natural resources. The word “kintsugi” means “golden joinery.” Historically, whenever the nee
arose, a skilled artisan would mend tea ceremony pottery with a special lacquer made from go
or silver powder. In modern times, more and more people are taking an interest in challengin
themselves to try kintsugi techniques. My own workshops in Japan, which I call “The Kintsug
Club,” were created for those curious about this unique art. It’s exciting to see this curiosity
taking hold in the West.
   In this book—just as I do in my workshops—I introduce both beginners and intermediate
kintsugi aficionados to a DIY approach to making lacquer and applying it using various kintsu
methods.

Four essential pillars of my approach:
1. Traditional: we will incorporate historically accurate techniques using real lacquer called
  “urushi”
2. Safe: we will ensure the least amount of harm, which means not using paint thinner or
  benzene
3. Enjoyable: it will be fun, easy-to-understand, streamlined
4. Economical: since mending is the goal, we will use kintsugi in the most cost-effective way

With the above in mind, my goal is that anyone will be able to learn kintsugi at home with
                                                      —Michihiro Horiaccessible materials and tools. Even if it takes a little extra time and effort, mending a much lov
piece with your own two hands is a joyful endeavor. I invite you to take a whole-hearted dive
into the art of kintsugi.

 becomes shards. Things that often break include ceramic spoons, porcelain
 cup handles, and tea pot spouts. Cracks and chips are common types of
 breakage.

About Urushi-buro
The Urushi-buro or “lacquer bath” is a small
wooden cupboard-like structure that has been used
since olden times to allow lacquer to sit in humidity
as it dries and cures. Shaped like a deep shoe
cabinet, there is an adjustable interior frame and                                                                                             Urushi-buro
shelf. Although you may not be able to easily acquire
a traditional urushi-buro, any wooden box or even
a cardboard box will do the trick. We recommend a
cube-shaped cardboard box that can be ventilated.
Avoid using plastic as the trapped humidity may
result in molding.

Using humidity to cure the lacquer
The drying or “curing” method for lacquer is not
the same as drying laundry. The curing involves
an enzymatic process: the Laccase enzyme in
the lacquer absorbs the moisture in the air and
oxidizes to harden. In order for the lacquer to
cure thoroughly, it’s important to pay attention to
the temperature and humidity levels. To promote
oxidization, you will need to add moisture to the
box as shown below. Place a thermometer and
hygrometer inside the box to monitor and maintain
optimal curing conditions.

Expert Tips

About Urushi Rash
Urushi rash occurs when the lacquer adheres to the skin and
causes an allergic reaction, similar to the reaction caused
by poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac. The severity
of the reaction depends on an individual’s sensitivity as
well as on the season. Reactions seem more common in the
summertime due to increased metabolism and active sweat
glands. We recommend wearing clothing that covers areas
that could come in contact with lacquer.

If lacquer adheres to the skin
Should your skin come in contact with lacquer, immediately
use vegetable oil to wipe it off. Lacquer is not water-soluble.
Once home, take a bath or shower as soon as possible, and use
something like a pumice stone to scrub off any remaining lacquer.

Urushi rash symptoms
There is usually an incubation period of about one week from point of contact. You may
initially experience itchiness on soft body parts such as your eyelids, neck, feet, hands or
stomach, followed by a rash with pustules and discharge. The symptoms will peak in a few
days, and the rash typically subsides in about ten days without leaving scars. Lacquer is not
toxic and, like seasonal allergies, when there is an abundance of the triggering material, the
symptoms will emerge.

What should I do if I get a rash?
Please see a dermatologist right away. The application of prescriptive corticosteroid seems to
be the most effective way to reduce inflammation. If the symptoms are severe, there is also the
option of oral or injected corticosteroids.
※ Although there is no medical evidence that immunity can develop for urushi rash, roughly 90%
  people affected by the rash do not have recurrences.
※ Note that a doctor without knowledge of lacquer may prescribe standard steroids which may not
   effective.
※ That said, please be aware that there is no medication specifically for urushi rash.

Home Remedies
• Baking soda and water paste (about 2-1 ratio)
• “Muhi S Cream” has immediate and effective anti-inflammatory impact. This is a
  Japanese anti-itch product available through several online vendors in the US.
• A warm colloidal oatmeal bath
• Rubbing alcohol or witch hazel
• Calendula or chamomile oil
• In warmer weather, don’t give into the temptation to work in short sleeves. To prevent
 urushi rash, it is best to avoid exposing your skin.
• Applying ointments like Nivea or Vaseline beforehand may have some preventative effects.

How to Clean Supplies
Always clean and put away your tools and supplies after
each use. Keep in mind that lacquer cannot be cleaned
with water. Oil must be used. In general, there are two
types of oils: ① non-drying oil ② drying oil. Each has
its own particular uses.

                                                                                 Even clean-up is
                                                                                              part of kintsugi.




How to clean brushes
Use non-drying oils such as canola/vegetable and olive
oils to clean brushes. First, place a dollop of oil the size
of a quarter coin on the glass sheet. Swish the dirty
brush in the oil, then place the brush tip on a different
part of the glass sheet and use a stick to squeeze out the
oil from the brush hairs. Repeat this 6 or 7 times until
the squeezed oil becomes clear. Even a tiny amount of
lacquer remaining on the brush hairs will harden and
damage the brush, rendering it unusable. Once the
brush has been cleaned, generously load the brush with
clean oil and store.

Expert Tips

About Precious Metal Powders

Ginfun/silver powder, suzufun/copper powder, and
shinchuufun/brass powder all have their own unique
properties and luster. Considering the mending project’s
design and vibe when choosing the finishing powder is an
additional way of enjoying kintsugi.

Silver
The discoloration and darkening commonly found in aging
silverware is not actually oxidation but sulphuration. The patina
evokes Ibushigin or the Japanese concept of subdued beauty.



   The timing for applying precious metal powder
     Although you could immediately apply the metallic
    powder after painting the lacquer layer, curing the lacquer
      for about 15 to 30 minutes in the urushi-buro will enable
     the powder to adhere better. Also, curing prevents the
    powder from sinking into the lacquer, which means you
      will end up using less precious powder.

    Aoiki

     Conversely, if breathing on the surface results in fogging
      (like blowing on a glass window on a cold day), the
     lacquer is too dry for the metallic powder to adhere. You
      will need to water wash with 800 grit sandpaper and paint
     another layer of lacquer.

Missed spots
There are occasions when you’ve reached the final stages of polishing the metallic powder
and you will notice that you missed some spots or that some sections are uneven. This is
particularly common when there are a number of places to apply the powder. Luckily, it’s
possible to fix these issues without redoing everything.

① Where there is not enough powder, apply a fresh coat of red lacquer on the exposed areas.
② Cure for 15 minutes, then apply the same type of powder to the newly cured lacquer.
③ Cure in the urushi-buro.
  From this point, repeat the polishing steps. It’s normal to perform these types of fixes.
  You could even say that the ease of touch-up is one of kintsugi’s many appeals.





Taikiba    Inukiba      and
Some people use a tool called taikiba, which means “red
snapper teeth,” for the funmaki step to apply the finishing
powder. Some others like to use something called inukiba which
utilize dogs’ teeth. These tools are gentler than the burnishing
sticks made out of stones such as agate.

If you are unable to acquire a taikiba or inukiba, an agate
burnishing stick can be ordered from stores specializing in
metalwork supplies.

Q & A
In this section we compiled common questions and discussion points that
come up in the Kintsugi Club.


Q1 About how much is the initial investment for kintsugi?
If you mend with precious metal powders other than gold, you can start with about US$35–45. Kinpun/
gold powder varies in price, since the cost of precious metal fluctuates and costs vary by vendor, but a
gram is approximately US$100. Shinchuufun/brass powder is a low-budget option.


Q2 What would be considered beautiful kintsugi?
It is entirely subjective, of course, but kintsugi tends to look better when the painted lines are delicate.
At the same time, the purpose of kintsugi is to repair and reinforce, so it doesn’t necessarily follow that
the thinner the line, the better. “Does it look strange?” “Is it too dominant?” “Is (the mended section)
too lumpy or uneven?” You will gradually be able to understand and address these types of questions as
you become familiar with the process and experience each type of mending project.


Q3 Is there a supplier of kintsugi materials? Do you have any
recommendations?
There are many websites (and the number is growing) where both traditional and synthetic kintsugi
materials are sold. Check fine art supply stores as well. You may also be able to find many of the
materials in the woodworking and paint supplies sections of home improvement stores. Note that the
commonly sold shin-urushi is easy for beginners to use, but it is a synthetic lacquer. For brushes, I
recommend the ones meant for applying powder or any brand of paint brush in size 0. Menso brushes
are okay too. If you invest in better quality, your brushes will last longer and you’ll save n the long run.


Q4 Are there certain materials suited or not suited for kintsugi?
Kintsugi is best suited for glazed earthenware and ceramic/porcelain pieces. When pottery is unglazed,
the lacquer tends to soak and leak which makes the kintsugi process difficult. Glass and lacquer
typically do not work well together, but can be an excellent challenge for intermediate level kintsugi
practitioners.

Unopened, a tube of lacquer usually lasts about a year. The curing capacity of lacqueras you need.declines with
time, especially after summer. However, adding fresh lacquer will boost the curing strength, and
placing the lacquer tube in the refrigerator will prevent deterioration (I was taught that there is no such
thing as lacquer that doesn’t cure). Regardless, lacquer will always cure with enough time, so take the
long view and enjoy the process of kintsugi.

Q6 What is the difference between synthetic adhesives and lacquer?
These days many people choose a style of kintsugi using synthetic adhesives, such as epoxy, which are
easier to use and cure faster. There are a couple of ways to incorporate synthetic materials into kintsugi:
① Gluing fragments with a synthetic glue or resin and finishing with gold-colored paint.
② Using lacquer and precious metal powder for just the finishing steps.

Method ① is effectively a shortcut and the kintsugi could be completed in a day. However, some
synthetic adhesives are not food safe, which will need to be taken into consideration. Method ② will
result in a very durable repair; however, what if the lacquer is damaged or peels off after a while? The
drawbacks of synthetic adhesives are that the very strength of the glue makes subsequent repairs
difficult and the transparency is tricky to manage. Synthetic resin is essentially paint. Some people
wonder if it’s wise to mend pottery meant for food with potentially toxic glue. If you decide to use a
synthetic adhesive, consider an epoxy glue introduced on page 75.
Then again, lacquer has its own shortcomings: some people have allergic reactions, curing takes a long
time, it doesn’t work well with glass, etc. Synthetic adhesives may be the best solution for items made
out of glass, and in any case, it’s important to weigh the pros and cons of the available materials for
kintsugi. To clarify your choices, I recommend asking questions such as, “Is it safe for my child?” “How
do I want to approach this precious piece of pottery?”

Q7 What are different ways to enjoy kintsugi?
Kintsugi is fundamentally a mending technique and can be applied to virtually anything that lacquer
will adhere to. Try kintsugi with chopstick rests, accessories, knick knacks…there are plenty of options.

Q9 I want to redo the kintsugi that I applied with synthetic glue.
Most adhesives will soften or melt in high heat, so try simmering the item in a pot of
water for 1 to 2 hours. Sometimes the kintsugi will disintegrate. If not, that means that
the glue is extra strong and if you try to forcibly pull apart the repaired area, another
part may break or crack. Simply leave the glued section as is and redo the lacquer and
finishing powder.

Q10 I accidentally got debris in the lacquer.
Use a filter for lacquer (miyoshinogami) to strain the debris. You can filter the lacquer as many times as
you need to.


Q11 It’s challenging to paint thin lacquer lines.
If the lacquer on the glass sheet is lumpy and hard, it will be difficult to apply it in smooth, delicate
lines. Add a little bit of turpentine oil or camphor oil to dilute the lacquer. Both are plant-based
solvents. Only add a very small amount of the oil (less than a rain drop, for example), because diluting
the lacquer weakens it, resulting in a less durable finish.

Q12 Can I use gold leaf instead of kinpun/gold powder?
There are some kintsugi techniques that use gold leaf, but compared to a kinpun/gold powder finish,
gold leaf tends to have less density. Gold leaf is more suitable for wall surfaces or as decorative elements
and tends to peel off easily. It may not be the best option for mending.

Q14 I was taught to clean brushes with nail polish remover or paint thin
is that okay?
I advise against it because they will damage the brushes. For the sake of the brushes and for
your own health, I highly recommend using only vegetable oils. Because lacquer will naturally
harden, after cleaning the brush hairs thoroughly, load the it with clean oil. Some people like
to clean brushes with paint thinner or other potent cleansers to remove the oiliness before
using it to paint, but I’ve found that wiping the brush hairs with a rag is sufficient.

Conclusion


As the quality of life increases, there has been a profusion of high quality
pottery and of artists producing beautiful work. There has also been a
proportional increase in the appreciation of kintsugi. In modern times,
convenient adhesives are readily available and the process of kintsugi has
been evolving and diversifying.

Out of the many options available, the ultimate decision is up to you. No
matter which techniques or materials are used, I believe that the most
important considerations are, “Is it comfortable and safe?” and “Does this
enrich my life?” As with all art forms, the methods and supplies have less
to do with the results than the care and emotions infused into the projects.
Kintsugi is not just about simple repairs, but is an expression of kindness
and love. You can redo the repairs as many times as needed or as desired, so
there is no such thing as failure with kintsugi. You just try, and try again. It is
an apt metaphor for making dreams come true, and kintsugi teaches us the
power of resilience.

I hope that this book will open up the world of kintsugi to you and be a
source of mending and enriching of your own life.

                                       —Michihiro Hori

Preface﻿

The reference book Additive Manufacturing of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic
Matrix Composites: Current Status and Future Developments is a contribution to the
field of additive manufacturing (AM), providing a detailed examination of the cur­
rent state and future potential of ceramic AM. Its comprehensive coverage, technical
depth, and future-oriented discussion make it a significant resource for researchers
and industry professionals interested in the advancements and applications of AM in
ceramics. The book stands out as a thorough and informative piece of work in this
domain. It serves as an excellent reference for anyone interested in understanding the
potential and challenges of this technology in the ceramics industry.
   This book provides a detailed insight into AM of advanced ceramics through
systematic well-structured chapters of the book for each AM technology, in terms of
final density, surface finish, and mechanical properties. An in-depth analysis of the
opportunities, issues, advantages, and limitations arising when processing advanced
ceramics is also provided. It aims to discuss the future trends and potential develop­
ments in this rapidly growing area of materials science.
   This book focuses on the latest advances in the AM of ceramics and presents
the historical origins and evolution of each related technique. The main technical
aspects, including feedstock properties, process control, and post-treatments, are
also discussed. The technical challenges and advice about how to address these are
presented. Comparisons are made between the techniques to facilitate the selection
of the best ones for practical use. In addition, representative applications of the AM
of various types of ceramics are surveyed. Future directions are pointed out on the
advancement of materials and forming mechanisms for the fabrication of high-per­
formance ceramic components.
  The book in hand is written specifically for undergraduates in mechanical,
industrial, manufacturing, and materials engineering disciplines at the second
to fourth levels to cover AM technology related to the courses of manufacturing
technology taught in engineering colleges and institutions all over the world. It
also covers the needs of production and manufacturing engineers and technolo­
gists participating in related industries. Additionally, it can be used by students in
other disciplines concerned with design and manufacturing, such as automotive,
biomedical, and aerospace engineering. The book stands out as a thorough and
informative piece of work in this domain. It serves as an excellent reference for
anyone interested in understanding the potential and challenges of this technology
in the ceramics industry. The book’s thorough coverage and technical depth make
it a valuable reference that will serve as a guide for both academic study and prac­
tical application.
  As the field of ceramic AM continues to evolve, this book looks ahead to the
future, identifying key trends and potential developments that will shape the industry
in the coming years. Topics such as the integration of AM with Industry 4.0, the rise
of sustainable manufacturing practices, and the potential for large-scale production

of ceramic components are explored in detail. This future-oriented discussion not
only highlights the ongoing advancements but also encourages readers to think crit­
ically about the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead.
   In conclusion, this book is a thorough and informative work that significantly
contributes to the understanding and advancement of AM in ceramics. It is our hope
that this book will inspire continued innovation and exploration in this exciting field,
fostering the development of new technologies and applications that will shape the

  The language of AM is one of the barriers to entry into the AM techniques.
Designers, process developers, computer modelers, laser specialists, motion control

Considering this, particular attention is paid to providing acronyms at the beginning

CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION TO ADDITIVE
MANUFACTURING (AM)

Introduces and defines the additive manufacturing techniques (AMTs) and provides
the concept and features of this new technology.

CHAPTER 2: AM OF ADVANCED CERAMICS

Presents the use of additive manufacturing (AM) of advanced ceramics in the cre­
ation of complex, high-performance parts. These materials, known for their strength
and thermal stability, are processed using direct AM (single-step) and indirect AM
(multi-step). AM offers design flexibility and reduced material waste, but challenges

Preface                                                                                      xi

persist in achieving precision, material consistency, and efficient post-processing.
Cost comparisons with traditional methods like injection molding highlight both
benefits and limitations, especially for mass production. Additionally, environmental
and health concerns, such as toxic emissions, remain important considerations in the
AM of ceramics. Despite these hurdles, AM holds significant potential for advancing
ceramic applications.

CHAPTER 3: FEEDSTOCK MATERIALS FOR AMC

Presents the feedstock forms for AMC, ceramic powder preparation, and pow­
der-based AM of ceramics. It describes the ceramic feedstocks and binders for AM.
Photopolymers and additives such as photoinitiators, surfactants, plasticizers, stabi­
lizers, dispersants, crosslinkers, rheological modifiers, and de-binders are presented.
Polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) represent a promising class of materials formed
by the pyrolysis of preceramic polymers (PCPs). These materials are synthesized
using Si-based preceramic polymers, which allow for the creation of high-perfor­
mance ceramics with tailored properties. Key types of preceramic polymers include
polysilazanes, polysiloxanes, and polycarbosilanes, each offering unique advantages
in terms of stability, strength, and heat resistance. Recent advances and future devel­
opments of PDCs are well presented.

CHAPTER 4: CLASSIFICATION OF AM
PROCESSES OF CERAMIC MATERIALS

Offers an overview of the classification of additive manufacturing processes for
ceramic materials (AMC), providing a foundation for a deeper understanding of this
versatile technology and its potential applications. Classifying AMC processes based
on the type of feedstock material offers the most effective framework for exploring
the topics in the following chapters.

CHAPTER 5: SLURRY-BASED DEPOSITION
FOR ADVANCED CERAMICS﻿

Provides a detailed explanation of the methodologies behind Slurry-based Deposition
for Advanced Ceramics, showcasing various ceramic structures produced by each
method for different applications. It focuses on different additive manufacturing
techniques (AMTs), exploring their use in ceramic processing, along with their ben­
efits and challenges. The slurry-based AM of ceramics generally includes the disper­
sion of ceramic particles as feedstock in a liquid or semi-liquid system, in either inks
or pastes, which depend on the viscosity and solid loading of the system. Another
development is the use of PCP precursors as feedstock materials, not only for slur­
ry-based technologies but also for other additive manufacturing (AM) technologies,
as will be presented in the subsequent chapters.

xii                                                                    Preface

CHAPTER 6: POWDER-BASED DEPOSITION
FOR ADVANCED CERAMICS

Describes the powder-based deposition technique for advanced ceramics and their
feedstock design. It presents the multi-step AM technologies used to shape advanced
ceramics including binder jetting (BJ) or 3DP technology and powder-based binder
jetting (P-BJ). On the other hand, powder bed fusion (PBF), such as direct pow­
der-based selective laser sintering (P-dSLS), powder-based indirect selective laser
sintering (P-iSLS), and laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) discussed. Directed energy
deposition (DED) is also presented. The chapter includes review questions.

CHAPTER 7: BULK SOLID-BASED DEPOSITION FOR
ADVANCED CERAMICS

Explores bulk solid-based deposition methods for advanced ceramics and the design
of their feedstocks. It covers material extrusion (ME) techniques, including fused
filament fabrication (FFF) and fused granules. It provides details on the fused depo­
sition modeling (FDM) process. Additionally, it introduces robocasting (RC), freeze-
form extrusion fabrication (FEF), multiphase jet solidification (MJS), and ceramic
on-demand extrusion (CODE).  It highlights the advantages and limitations of
ceramic extrusion techniques. It discusses sheet lamination (SL) and the traditional
and computer-aided manufacturing of laminated engineering materials (CAM-
LEM), emphasizing the benefits and drawbacks of sheet lamination. The chapter
also presents various feedstocks containing preceramic precursors used for FDM
and direct ink writing (DIW).

CHAPTER 8: CHALLENGES, COMPARISON, AND PROCESS
SELECTION REGARDING AMC

Presents unique challenges due to the material’s inherent properties, such as brittle­
ness and high melting points. Key challenges include achieving desired part density,
resolution, and surface finish, while also minimizing post-processing requirements.
Selection criteria for AM processes include the specific ceramic material being
printed, part resolution, and final density, as well as geometric complexity and sur­
face finish. Additionally, post-processing techniques, including sintering and pol­
ishing, are essential for improving part quality. Considerations of manufacturing
costs, including material consumption and time, also play a significant role in pro­
cess selection. Understanding these factors is crucial to optimizing AMC processes,
ensuring high-performance and cost-effective production.

CHAPTER 9: AM OF CERAMIC MATRIX COMPOSITES (CMCS)

Presents the additive manufacturing (AM) of ceramic matrix composites (CMCs)
that enabled the production of highly customized, geometrically complex, and func­
tionalized parts with significantly improved properties and functionality, compared

Preface                                                                                                  xiii

to single-phase ceramic components. It also opens up a new way to shape dam­
age-tolerant ceramic composites with co-continuous phase reinforcement inspired by
natural materials. Nowadays, a large variety of AM techniques has been successfully
applied to fabricate CMCs, but variable properties have been obtained so far. This
chapter provides a comprehensive review of the AM of ceramic matrix composites
through a systematic evaluation of the capabilities and limitations of each AM tech­
nique, with an emphasis on reported results regarding the properties and potentials
of AM-manufactured ceramic matrix composites


CHAPTER 10 : POST-PROCESSING IN AMC PROCESSES

Post-processing is crucial in additive manufacturing (AM) of advanced ceramics
to improve material properties, surface finish, and dimensional accuracy. AM pro­
cesses often result in defects like porosity and residual stresses, affecting the final
product’s performance. Techniques such as heat treatment, polishing, and infiltration
help address these issues. The stair-stepping effect reduces surface resolution, neces­
sitating post-processing for refinement. Different AM methods (SLA, FDM, DIW,
PBF, BJ, MJ, LOM, DED) require specific post-processing approaches. Challenges
include maintaining feature integrity, achieving uniformity, and scaling processes
for industrial use.


CHAPTER 11 : DESIGN FOR ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING
OF ADVANCED CERAMICS

Explains the design for liquid slurry-based deposition for advanced ceramics, includ­
ing design for stereolithography (SLA), design for digital light processing (DLP),
and design for material jetting (MJ). It also describes these recommendations in the
design for powder-based deposition for advanced ceramics such as design for binder
jetting (BJ) and powder bed fusion (PBF): for example, laser beam melting and selec­
tive laser sintering (LBM and SLS). It presents the design recommendations for bulk
solid-based deposition of advanced ceramics, such as laminated object manufactur­
ing (LOM), and fused deposition modeling (FDM).


CHAPTER 12: INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS AND FUTURE TRENDS
OF AMC AND AM-CMCS

AM of advanced ceramics has emerged as a transformative technology in vari­
ous sectors, including aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical industries.
Presently, AM enables the fabrication of complex ceramic components with enhanced
design flexibility and reduced material waste. In aerospace, it allows the creation of
lightweight, high-performance parts for engines and thermal barriers. In medical
fields, AM of ceramics facilitates the production of custom implants and prosthet­
ics with improved biocompatibility. Looking to the future, the integration of AM
with advanced materials, such as functionally graded ceramics and multi-material

nents with tailored properties. The continuous improvement in AM technologies,
such as increased printing speed, precision, and material diversity, will likely open
up new opportunities in industries.

1.1  INTRODUCTION TO ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING

Writing a book on “additive manufacturing of ceramic materials” presents a chal­
lenge without first exploring the fundamentals of additive manufacturing (AM) as
a transformative technology. This technology, which emerged toward the end of the
twentieth century, was pioneered by Charles Hull from the USA and Kodama from
Japan. To provide a proper foundation for readers, especially those less familiar with
AM, this chapter introduces the concept of this new technology. To assist with under­
standing, we have included a list of acronyms at the beginning and a comprehensive
index at the end of the book for easy reference.
  The progress and features of the Industrial Revolution are illustrated in Figure 1.1.
Today, in the early decades of the twenty-first century, AM is becoming an integral
part of the ongoing Fourth Industrial Revolution. This new technological mode of
manufacturing offers broad flexibility for materials science, process development, and
structural design. Using AM, intricate and complex parts can be manufactured with
the desired quality, which would be extremely challenging using earlier subtractive
(machining) and formative (casting) manufacturing modes. Moreover, the inherent
nature of AM is leading manufacturing toward fully automated digital manufac­
turing. In contrast to earlier manufacturing techniques, which steadily evolved and
advanced in response to challenges experienced by earlier versions, AM is an entirely
new technique. Therefore, AM may be considered not an evolution but the dawn of
a new manufacturing era. Before diving deep into the technical features and current
status of AM, we examine its intriguing fundamental nature in the following sections.

1.1.1  Concept of AM

In the early decades of the twenty-first century, AM became a key component of
the ongoing Fourth Industrial Revolution. This advanced manufacturing technique
offers extensive flexibility in materials science, process innovation, and structural
design. With AM, complex and intricate parts can be produced with precision and
quality that would be nearly impossible with traditional subtractive (machining) or
formative (casting) methods. Additionally, AM’s inherent capabilities are steering
manufacturing toward fully automated digital production using robotic systems.
Unlike earlier manufacturing techniques that evolved through incremental advance­
ments, AM represents a completely new approach to manufacturing. Thus, it can be
seen not as an evolution but as the beginning of a new era in manufacturing. Before
exploring the technical aspects and current state of AM of advanced ceramics, let’s
first provide an overview of AM in the following introductory section.

   Although AM seems to be a new manufacturing mode in the twenty-first century,
it has existed silently as an auxiliary manufacturing technique for several decades in
the previous century. Eventually, AM was conceived as a fabrication method in the
polymeric system in 1981 by Hideo Kodama, from Japan (Kodama, 1981). He devel­
oped and demonstrated a prototype of the automatic fabrication of intricately shaped
polymers, using layer-by-layer curing of the liquid and photo-hardening the polymer
with ultraviolet (UV) rays. Charles Hull later advanced this technique and patented it
as stereolithography (SLA) (Hull, 1984). The concept of layer-upon-layer fabrication
was then coupled with existing metallic welding and surface coating techniques,
leading to various metallic AM techniques. Later, different AM approaches were
developed to form ceramic coatings on metallic substrates to improve materials’
wear, corrosion, and heat resistance.
  The American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM, an international stan­
dard organization primarily involved in developing and publishing voluntarily
consensus technical standards for a broad range of materials, techniques, services,
products, and systems) defines AM as “a process of joining materials to make parts
from 3D model data, usually layer upon layer, as opposed to subtractive manufac­
turing and formative manufacturing methodologies” (ASTM, 2015). Any material
in its pure continuum or bulk form is held together by atomic bonds; for example,
metals or alloys are bonded by metallic bonds, polymers by covalent and van der

Introduction to Additive Manufacturing (AM)                             3

Waals bonds, ceramics by ionic or covalent bonds, and composites by any combi­
nation of these bonds. AM involves joining the material using a distinct physical
phenomenon associated with an energy source that leads to the formation of such
primary atomic bonds. The energy source can be in any of the forms (laser beam,
electron beam, ultrasound, or friction); it is transformed into heat or a combination of
heat and mechanical energy that joins the material through a primary atomic bond.
This joining takes place at a micro- to macro-dimensional scale, depending on the
type of energy source and the size and shape of the pieces of material. These pieces
of material in a feedstock can be in forms such as powder, liquid polymer, wires,
rods, bars, and sheets. A moving interaction zone of energy and feedstock forms a
single consolidated or joined track/line of material. The successive joining of such
tracks in a single plane forms a fabricated layer of a given material. Eventually, this
layer-upon-layer consolidation results in a three-dimensional component, and hence
the name additive manufacturing was coined.
  The emergence of AM is regarded as a manufacturing revolution. AM is a series
of advanced manufacturing technologies used to fabricate physical parts in a discrete
point-by-point, line-by-line, or layer-by-layer additive manner from 3D computer-
aided design (CAD) models that are digitally sliced into 2D cross-sections. AM is
a unique manufacturing philosophy that enables the flexible preparation of highly
complex and precise structures that are difficult to realize using traditional fabrica­
tion methods such as casting and machining. Productivity can also be significantly
increased, as many objects can be built in a single run. As a result, AM has rapidly
gained attention across the science and engineering communities since its emergence
in the 1980s.
 AM allows the flexibility of fabricating any intricate shape that can be created
with the aid of CAD software. A virtual model of the part to be fabricated is con­
verted into an STL (derived from STereroLithography; it is also sometimes defined
as Standard Triangulation Language or Standard Tessellation Language) file format,
which presents the geometry in a form the AM machines can understand to build the
physical part. The STL file allows the AM machine to read the path of the interaction
zone of energy and feedstock in each layer, as well as the dimensions and the number
of layers to fabricate the geometry encrypted in the STL file. Given this path and the
geometric dimensions, the machine allows the user to choose processing parameters
such as power and the speed of the moving energy source. The feedstock provides
additional flexibility depending on the material type, shape, and size distribution.
  The various components of AM provide tremendous process flexibility, and their
combination can lead to multiple possible fabrication outcomes. These features of
AM are as follows:

   •  Type of energy source
   •  Physical phenomenon
   •  Type of material (metal, ceramic, polymer, composite) and its composition
   •  Type of feedstock (shape, size, and distribution)
   •  Means of distributing the feedstock to interact with the energy source
   •  Combination of processing parameters (power of energy source, speed, and
      path of energy-feedstock interaction zone and feedstock input)

1.1.2   Techniques of AM Categorized According to the ASTM

There are lots of individual AM processes which vary in their method of layer
manufacturing. Individual processes will differ depending on the material and
machine technology used. The ASTM group, “ASTM F42 – Additive Manufacturing,”
formulated a set of standards that classify the range of AM processes into seven cate­
gories, ASTM-2009. These are vat polymerization (VP), material jetting (MJ), mate­
rial extrusion (ME), powder bed fusion (PBF), binder jetting (BJ), directed energy
deposition (DED), and sheet lamination (SL) (Figure 1.2).
    It’s important to provide definitions and brief descriptions of the seven AM cate­
gories according to ASTM/ISO standards.

    1. BJ: This is the technology that gave 3D printing (3DP) its name, since it
      uses inkjet printer heads that selectively bind powder together. An adhe­
      sive is selectively deposited on a powder bed using standard inkjet printing
      (IJP) technology and binds or “glues” the particles together. Any powder not
     touched by the binder is shaken, blown, or brushed off the finished part.
   2. DED: A feedstock, usually in powder form, is fed into a directed energy
     beam, typically a laser. The feedstock material melts and re-solidifies, creat­
      ing a solid part. The work blank formed by DED relies on CNC machining
      to achieve the required precision.
     3. ME: A feedstock material is forced through a nozzle and hardens or solidi­
       fies upon deposition. It is a low-cost AM method, which uses relatively cheap
      materials and does not pose the risk of toxic gas and chemical pollution.
   4. MJ: Droplets of material are selectively deposited using IJP technology to
     form a solid part. Again, this uses inkjet technology, but this time using
      material to selectively deposit where needed.
   5. PBF: A heat source, usually a laser or electron beam, selectively scans a
     powder bed and fuses the powder particles together. PBF possesses fast
     manufacturing speed and a high material utilization rate and can be used in
     a wide range of materials.

    6. SL: Sheets of feedstock are cut in the required shape and then stacked
      together or vice versa. Strictly speaking, this technology is subtractive, but
      since it builds layer by layer, it slips in as an additive process. It works using
     a sheet of paper or plastic (or any sheet material), which is cut by a laser or
      scalpel into shape, and the next sheet layer is cut to size and shape and stuck
    down on top of it.
    7. VP: A liquid photopolymer is selectively exposed to a low-power UV light
      source. The UV light causes the photopolymer to crosslink locally, and a
      solid part is formed. VP can produce prototypes with high surface quality
     and dimensional accuracy and complex geometry.

Even though there are seven AM process categories, their principles are similar.
Typically, any AM process involves three primary steps (Figure 1.3):

    1. A digital model design – a process that uses CAD software to create a 3D
       digital model. The working of 3D printers, as shown in Figure 1.3 (Jandyal
       et al., 2022), is based on the fact that they are designed to read the Standard
      Tessellation Language (STL) file type. An STL file stores information about
    3D models. This format describes only the surface geometry of a three-
     dimensional object without any representation of color, texture, or other
    common model attributes. The STL file format is the most commonly used
        file format for 3DP. When used in conjunction with a 3D slicer, it allows
     a computer to communicate with 3D printer hardware. Since its humble
      beginnings, the STL file format has been adopted and supported by many
      other CAD software packages, and today, it is widely used for rapid proto­
      typing, 3DP, and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM).
    2. Processing (printing) is a manufacturing process in which the digital model
       is transferred to a 3D printer, and the physical object is printed using various
      parameters. As a 3D printed object is fabricated layer by layer, each consec­
      utive layer has to be supported by the platform, the preceding layer, or extra
      support elements. After the correct and optimal orientation of the model and
      the supports has been designed, the STL model, including the supports, is
      sliced into layers with a plane parallel to the platform surface, namely, the
           ﻿x–y plane. Each layer is then built consecutively in the z-direction. The layer
      thickness depends on the printer, AM technology, and quality requirements.

1.1.3   Integration of AM with Other Advanced Technologies﻿

Currently, the direct fabrication of functional end-use products is becoming the main
trend of AM technology, and it has been increasingly implemented to manufacture
parts in small or medium quantities. It is important to understand that AM was not
developed in isolation from other related technologies. For example, it would not
be possible for AM to exist without innovations in areas like 3D graphics and CAD
software. Aside from computer technology, there are a number of other technologies
that have been developed along with AM that are worthy of note here, since they have
served to contribute to further improvement of AM systems. These related technolo­
gies include (Gibson et al., 2021):

    1. Lasers: Many of the earliest AM systems were based on laser technology.
     The reasons are that lasers provide a high-intensity and highly collimated
    beam of energy that can be moved very quickly in a controlled manner
     with the use of directional mirrors. Since AM requires the material in each
      layer to be solidified or joined in a selective manner, lasers and similar heat
      sources are ideal candidates for use. There are two kinds of laser processing
     used in AM: curing and heating. With photopolymer resins, the require­
     ment is for laser energy of a specific frequency that will cause the liquid
      resin to solidify, or “cure.” Usually, this laser is in the UV range, but other
      frequencies can be used for heating requirements to provide sufficient ther­
     mal energy to cut through a layer of solid material, to cause powder to melt
      or sheets of material to fuse. For powder processes, for example, the key
       is to melt the material in a controlled fashion without creating too great a
      build-up of heat, so that when the laser energy is removed, the molten mate­
       rial rapidly solidifies again.
    2. Printing Technologies : Inkjet or droplet printing technology has rapidly
     developed in recent years. Improvements in resolution and reduction in
      costs have meant that high-resolution printing, often with multiple colors,
       is available as part of our everyday lives. Initially, colored inks were low in
      viscosity and fed into the printheads at ambient temperatures. Now, it is pos­
      sible to generate much higher pressures within the droplet formation cham­
      ber, so that materials with much higher viscosity and even molten materials
     can be printed. This means that droplet deposition can now be used to print
      photocurable and molten resins as well as binders for powder systems.
    3. Materials: Earlier AM technologies dealt with materials that were already
      available. However, these original materials were far from ideal for antici­
      pated new applications. For example, the early photocurable resins resulted
      in AM models that were brittle and warped easily. Powders degraded
      quickly, and many of the materials used resulted in parts that were quite
     weak. AM technology is capable of processing a wide variety of functional
      materials, including structural and conductive metals, ceramics, conductive
      adhesives, dielectrics, semiconductors, biological materials, and many other

8            AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

      materials used to fabricate aerospace, medical, and consumer electronic
      devices. Materials can even be blended during printing to create new alloys
      or gradient structures for improved product performance. Parts are now
    much more accurate, stronger, and longer lasting, and it is even possible to
      process metals and alloys with some AM technologies. These new materials
     have resulted in producing even higher-temperature materials and smaller
      feature sizes.
   4. Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs): The input CAD models for
   AM are large data files generated using standard computer technology. Once
      they are on the AM machine, however, these files are reduced to a series of
      process stages that require sensor input and signaling of actuators. Industrial
      microcontroller systems form the basis of PLCs, which are used to reliably
      control industrial processes.
    5. Computer Numerical Control (CNC): One of the reasons AM technology
     was originally developed was that CNC technology was not able to produce
      satisfactory output within the required time frames. CNC machining was
      slow, cumbersome, and difficult to operate. AM technology, on the other
      hand, was quite easy to set up with quick results but had poor accuracy and
      limited material capability. As improvements in AM technologies came about,
     vendors of CNC machining technology realized that there was now growing
      competition. For geometries that can be machined using a single setup orien­
       tation, CNC machining is often the fastest, most cost-effective method. For
      parts with complex geometries or parts that require a large proportion of the
      overall material volume to be machined away as scrap, AM can be used to
     produce the part more quickly and economically than when using CNC.
   6. Robotics: AM is integrated with robotics to enhance the flexibility, pre­
      cision, and scalability of the manufacturing process. Robotics allows for
      the automation of AM, enabling the precise positioning of the print head
      or material deposition nozzle, which is critical for complex geometries or
      large-scale production. Robots can move in multiple axes, adjust orienta­
       tions, and access difficult areas of a part during the printing process, offering
      increased design freedom and efficiency. This integration also allows for the
     combination of AM with other operations, such as assembling, inspecting,
      or post-processing parts in a continuous, automated workflow. Furthermore,
      robotic systems can adapt to changes in the print environment, improving
     accuracy and reducing human intervention.
   7.  Artificial Intelligence (AI): AI plays a crucial role in enhancing the effi­
      ciency and quality of AM. AI is used for optimizing the design and print­
      ing process, such as predicting material behavior, detecting defects, and
     improving print paths for better accuracy. Machine learning algorithms can
      analyze data from sensors and monitoring systems during the printing pro­
      cess to identify patterns and anticipate potential issues, leading to real-time
      adjustments that prevent errors. AI also aids in process planning, ensuring
     optimal material usage and reducing waste, as well as improving quality

      control by automating inspection and testing of finished parts. Through AI,

   8. Internet of Things (IoT) Technologies: IoT sensors collect real-time data

      printing process. This data is analyzed to optimize operations, detect poten­

1.1.4  Comparison of AM to Conventional Manufacturing Techniques﻿

Compared to traditional manufacturing processes, the primary advantage of AM
is its ability to create complex designs with high accuracy in dimensions and struc­
tural features without the need for specific tooling or dies. In addition, almost all AM
techniques are faster than traditional processes without the need for further surface
finishing. However, AM is best suited for low-volume production of complex geome­
tries, because time and cost are fully independent of printed part complexity. A case
study performed by Atzeni and Salmi (2012) compared the cost of manufacturing an
aluminum aerospace component using high-pressure die casting and PBF processes.
Production volumes below 42 parts favor the AM PBF process due to the high cost and
long manufacturing time of the die. Further, AM affords the ability to make complex
geometries that are impossible to create through subtractive manufacturing or forming
processes. It is important to note that mechanical properties are largely anisotropic for
parts produced by AM, due to the layer-wise nature of the process (Gao et al., 2015).
  The fundamental difference between AM and conventional manufacturing is their
distinct processes and fabrication steps leading to the final component. Table 1.1
provides the key features that separate AM from conventional manufacturing.

   •  Material  Efficiency﻿: The prime  functional  difference between  these
     approaches arises from the substantially high material efficiency associated
     with the AM process, whereas conventional manufacturing results in more
      material loss through the subtractive approach in multiple steps.
   •  Complex Parts﻿: The layer-upon-layer approach of AM allows the fabrica­
      tion of complex geometries, which are nearly impossible or highly challeng­
      ing to fabricate using a conventional approach in a single processing step.
   •  Assembly Stage﻿: Traditionally, a moving system is required to manufacture
      in stages, first fabricating each component of the system and then assem­
      bling them. AM merges manufacturing and assembly into a single step,
     making a more efficient fabrication chain.
   •  Customized Printing﻿: AM provides the freedom to conceive any imagina­
      ble shape and make it a reality. In addition, customization through a digital
      interface allows personalized products to be made for individuals. Conven­
      tional manufacturing does not provide such customization or the freedom to
      fabricate any shape.

1.2  REVIEW QUESTIONS

1.2.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. What is Additive Manufacturing (AM)?
     Answer: Additive Manufacturing, or AM, is a process where objects are
       built layer by layer using digital designs. Unlike traditional methods,  it
      doesn’t need molds or tooling, which makes it great for creating complex
     shapes and custom parts.
    2. How is AM different from traditional subtractive manufacturing?﻿
     Answer: AM adds material to create a part, while subtractive manufacturing
     removes material – like cutting or drilling – from a solid block. AM is more
      material-efficient and better for intricate designs.
   3. What are the main benefits of AM?
     Answer: AM allows for greater design freedom, less material waste, faster
      prototyping, and easy customization. It also enables complex geometries
      that would be difficult or impossible with traditional methods.
    4. What are the main types of AM techniques according to ASTM?﻿
     Answer: According  to ASTM  standards, AM  includes  seven main
      categories:
       •   Material extrusion
       •  Vat polymerization
       •  Powder bed fusion

       •  Binder jetting
       •   Directed energy deposition
       •  Sheet lamination
       •   Material jetting
     Each has its own strengths depending on the material and application.
   5. How does material extrusion work?﻿
     Answer: This method heats a material – usually plastic – and pushes it
     through a nozzle to build the object layer by layer. It’s one of the most com­
    mon types of 3DP used today.
   6. What is powder bed fusion used for in AM?﻿
     Answer: Powder bed fusion uses a heat source, like a laser, to fuse lay­
      ers of powdered material into solid parts. It’s popular for printing high-
     performance metal, ceramic, or plastic components.
   7. How is vat polymerization different from other AM methods?﻿
     Answer: Vat polymerization uses a vat of liquid resin that’s cured with UV
       light. It offers excellent precision and smooth surfaces, making it ideal for
      detailed prototypes and small, intricate parts.
   8. What is directed energy deposition (DED)?﻿
     Answer: DED involves melting material – often metal – using a laser or
      electron beam as it’s deposited. It’s particularly useful for repairing existing
      parts or adding features to them.
   9. How is AM combined with robotics?﻿
     Answer: Robotics can enhance AM by automating complex tasks, allow­
      ing for multi-axis printing and the creation of large or intricate structures.
     Robots also improve precision and consistency.
  10. What role does AI play in AM?﻿
     Answer: AI helps optimize the printing process by planning efficient paths,
      predicting how materials will behave, and detecting defects in real-time.
     This leads to better quality and faster production.
  11. How does 3D scanning support AM?﻿
     Answer: 3D scanning captures the shape and dimensions of physical
      objects, which is useful for reverse engineering, quality inspection, or repli­
      cating existing parts with high accuracy.
  12. Can AM work with Internet of Things (IoT) technologies?﻿
     Answer: Absolutely. IoT devices can monitor the AM process in real-time,
      collect performance data, and even trigger maintenance alerts – making
      production smarter and more efficient.
  13. How does AM compare with traditional machining when it comes to
     material waste?﻿
     Answer: AM is much more efficient – it only uses the material needed to
      build the part, while traditional machining cuts away excess, generating
     more waste.
  14. What are the advantages of AM over injection molding?﻿
     Answer: AM doesn’t require molds, so it saves on tooling costs and time. It
      also allows for more complex designs and easier design changes, which is
      harder and costlier with injection molding.

2.1  HISTORICAL BACKGROUND OF AM OF ADVANCED
    CERAMICS

In the early beginnings (1980s–1990s), AM traces its origins back to 1980 when
Kodama Hideo 1980 from the Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute in
Japan invented the vat photopolymerization process. Kodama Hideo developed a
rapid, cost-effective, and automated method for creating three-dimensional parts
by selectively curing a liquid photo-hardening polymer using ultraviolet (UV) light.
Although this innovation represents the first documented success in AM, it failed to
gain commercial momentum, and Kodama’s patent lapsed before reaching approval.
   In 1984 Hull C patented and commercialized the first AM technology. He devel­
oped an “apparatus for production of three-dimensional parts by stereolithography,”
which was named SLA-1, Gornet and Wohlers, 2014. In addition to inventing the
machine and method, he created the SLA (an abbreviation of stereolithography)
file format to store geometric data for parts. This machine falls into the vat photo­
polymerization family of AM technologies. Hull (1984) developed the SLA-1 with
the intent of more efficiently producing prototypes. Closely following Hull’s pat­
ent, the selective laser sintering (SLS) process, a type of powder bed fusion, was
patented in 1986 by Deckard et al. They formed the company DMT based on their
SLS technology, which was later acquired by 3D Systems. In 1987, Masters patented
a process for ejecting particles or droplets or using a laser to attract material to a spe­
cific point to automatically create three-dimensional objects. Masters’ patent covers
both material jetting and direct energy deposition processes. The following year, the

2.1.1   Initial Exploration with Ceramics (1990s)

In the 1990s, researchers started investigating the application of ceramics in AM.
However, the high melting points and brittleness of ceramics presented considerable
challenges. Early efforts focused on modifying established polymer and metal AM
techniques to work with ceramic powders.
    Initially, Hull designed SLAs to fabricate photopolymers and extended their
application to ceramic fabrication in the 1990s. The SLA process entails a liquid
monomer–ceramic particle suspension within a vat, with the build stage moving
along the z-direction. A point laser or light source emitting UV-range wavelengths
cures the liquid precursor – a photopolymerizable monomer with homogeneously
dispersed ceramic particles of nano or micrometer size – onto the build plate as
per the design specified in the CAD file. The build stage progressively descends
throughout each layer, covering the preceding layer with the liquid precursor, fol­
lowed by laser curing. This iterative process continues until the completion of part
fabrication, yielding the green part – a cured photopolymer network with ceramic
particle inclusions. After fabrication, the green body undergoes post-processing,
which encompasses pyrolysis to remove the organics, leaving behind the ceramic
structure. This is followed by sintering the ceramic at high temperatures to achieve
a purely ceramic structure devoid of polymer traces. SLA’s versatility and precision
in ceramic fabrication have propelled its adoption across various industries, includ­
ing aerospace, automotive, and biomedical.2 As research advances and technology
evolves, SLA remains a leading 3DP technique for ceramic production, offering
intricate geometries and precise components that meet the demands of modern man­
ufacturing processes.
   In 1996, a groundbreaking advancement was introduced in the field of SLA
known as “DLP.” DLP, similar to SLA, operates by progressively lowering the build
stage with each layer. However, it distinguishes itself by employing a mask-based
UV light source, typically utilizing a liquid crystal display as the dynamic mask
generator. This innovation enabled rapid curing of entire layers of photopolymer­
izable liquid in moments, in contrast to the point curing method employed in tra­
ditional SLA. The utilization of ultrafast light switching and integral projection in

AM of Advanced Ceramics                                            21

DLP significantly reduces printing time compared with SLA. DLP achieves higher
resolutions for printed parts than conventional SLA methods. In DLP the maximum
achievable part height was initially constrained by the height of the build chamber.
A significant advancement in DLP technology was made to overcome this limitation,
replacing the top-bottom approach with a bottom-up approach. The key distinction
lies in the positioning of the digital light projector in the top-bottom approach, at
the bottom of the system, separated from the chamber by a glass window. The build
stage is inverted, and ensuring proper curing of the initial layer and its adhesion to
the build plate is crucial to prevent part failure (Chaudhary et al., 2022).
  Many factors, such as resin matrix and printing parameters, influence the quality
of the final part produced via SLA or DLP. Achieving accurate dimensionality, struc­
tural integrity, and surface quality necessitates meticulous optimizations. Printing
parameters such as layer thickness, exposure time of UV source, and scanning speed
further need optimizations along with resin matrix characteristics for a successful
printed green body part with accurate dimensionality, structural integrity, and sur­
face quality. The layer thickness determines the final resolution of the printed part.
The exposure time of the UV source governs the degree of polymerization and cur­
ing of the resin matrix. Precise exposure time control is essential to achieve uniform
curing and prevent under- or over-curing. The UV source’s scanning speed affects
the polymerization and curing rate (Chaudhary et al., 2022).
  Alumina (Al 2 O 3) and zirconia (ZrO2) are among the most commonly used
ceramic materials in SLA. These materials offer a combination of desirable mechan­
ical, thermal, and chemical properties, making them well-suited for a wide range of
applications across various industries.
 AM of ceramic materials has a rich history, characterized by the evolution of
various techniques and the development of new materials tailored for specific appli­
cations. The historical development of AM of ceramic materials reflects a trajec­
tory of overcoming significant material and technological challenges. From initial
adaptations of polymer and metal AM techniques to the development of specialized
methods, the field has seen substantial growth. Continued advancements in material
science and AM technology are likely to further expand the capabilities and applica­
tions of ceramic AM in the coming years.
   During the 1990s few new processes were developed, and efforts were made to
move toward higher process efficiency and production of end-use parts (Kruth et
al. 1998). The term “additive manufacturing” had already begun to replace “rapid
prototyping.” Six-fold and eight-fold decreases in process time for vat photopolymer­
ization and material extrusion, respectively, were realized during the 1990s (Kruth et
al., 1998). This decrease in processing time enabled a new wave of rapid throughput
manufacturing, where one-off parts could be ordered, manufactured, and shipped in
under 24 hours.

2.2  ADVANCED CERAMICS

Ceramics are inorganic, non-metallic materials typically organized into the follow­
ing categories based on their nature and industrial use: clays, whiteware, cements,
glasses, refractories, abrasives, and advanced ceramics. Advanced ceramics, also
called “technical,” “engineering,” or “fine” ceramics, are mainly polycrystalline
materials which, unlike traditional ceramics that are produced from natural sources,
are almost always synthetic in nature and/or have been engineered (high purity, tai­
lored particle size distribution, small grain size) to meet the service requirements
of increasingly more demanding industrial applications in fields as diverse as aero­
space, automotive, biomaterials, communications, transport, energy, and defense.
Their unique set of physical, chemical, and mechanical properties, including high
temperature resistance, superior hardness, high stiffness, low coefficient of friction,
and excellent chemical inertness, is a direct consequence of their atomic structure
based on rigid ionic and covalent bonds.
  The first materials used by humans were natural materials such as wood and
stone. The discovery that certain clays could be mixed, shaped, and hardened by
firing led to what was probably the first man-made material. Traditional ceramic
products, such as bricks and pottery, have continued to be key materials through­
out history. More recently, ceramic materials have assumed significant roles in
various engineering applications. Most of these utilize their outstanding physical
properties, including the ability to withstand high temperatures, provide a wide
variety of electrical and magnetic properties and resist wear. In general, ceram­
ics are hard, brittle, high-melting-point materials with low electrical and thermal
conductivity, low thermal expansion, good chemical and thermal stability, good
creep resistance, high elastic modulus, and high compressive strengths that are
retained at elevated temperatures. A family of “structural ceramics” has also
emerged, and these materials now provide enhanced mechanical properties that
make them attractive for many load-bearing applications. Glass and glass products
now account for about half of the ceramic materials market. Advanced ceramic
materials (including the structural ceramics, electrical and magnetic ceramics, and
fiber-optic material) compose another 20%. Whiteware and porcelain enameled
products (such as household appliances) account for about 10% each, while refrac­
tories and structural clay products make up most of the difference (Black and
Kohser, 2007).

24           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

  Advanced ceramics is an emerging technology with a broad base of current and
potential applications. The base materials currently include silicon nitride, silicon
carbide, partially stabilized zirconia, transformation-toughened zirconia, alumina,
sialons, boron carbide, boron nitride, titanium diboride, and ceramic composites.
The materials and products are characterized by high strength, high fracture tough­
ness, fine grain size, and little or no porosity. Applications include a wide variety
of wear-resistant parts (including bearings, seals, valves, and dies), cutting tools,
punches, dies, and engine components, as well as use in heat exchangers, gas tur­
bines, and furnaces. Porous products have been used as substrate material for cata­
lytic converters and as filters for streams of molten metal. Biocompatible ceramics
have been used as substitutes for joints and bones and as dental implants.
  Alumina ceramics are the most common for industrial applications. They are rel­
atively inexpensive and offer high hardness and abrasion resistance, low density, and
high electrical resistivity. Alumina is strong in compression and retains useful proper­
ties at temperatures as high as 1900°C, but it is limited by low toughness, low tensile
strength, and susceptibility to thermal shock and attack by highly corrosive media.
Due to its high melting point, it is generally processed in a powder form. Silicon
carbide and silicon nitride offer excellent strength and wear resistance with moderate
toughness. They work well in high-stress and high-temperature applications, such as
turbine blades, and may well replace nickel- or cobalt-based superalloys.

   Zirconia is inert to most metals and retains strength to temperatures well over
2200°C. Partially stabilized zirconia combines the zirconia characteristics of resis­
tance to thermal shock, wear, and corrosion; low thermal conductivity; and low
friction coefficient with the enhanced strength and toughness brought about by dop­
ing the material with oxides of calcium, yttrium, or magnesium. Transformation-
toughened zirconia has even greater toughness as a result of dispersed second
phases throughout the ceramic matrix. When a crack approaches the metastable
phase, it transforms to a more stable structure, increasing in volume to compress
and stop the crack.
  The high cost of the structural ceramics continues to be a barrier to their wide­
spread acceptance. High-grade ceramics are currently several times more expensive
than their metal counterparts. Even factoring in enhanced lifetime and improved
performance, there is still a need to reduce cost. Work continues, however, toward
the development of a low-cost, high-strength, high-toughness ceramic with a useful
temperature range. Parallel efforts are underway to ensure flaw detection in the range
of 10 to 50 mm. If these efforts are successful, ceramics could compete where tool
steels, powdered metals, coated materials, and tungsten carbide are now being used.
Potential applications include engines, turbochargers, gas turbines, bearings, pump
and valve seals, and other products that operate under high-temperature, high-stress
environments.
  A ceramic automobile engine has been discussed for a number of years. By allow­
ing higher operating temperatures, engine efficiency could be increased. Sliding fric­
tion would be reduced, and there would be no need for cooling. The radiator, water
pump, coolant, fan belt, and water lines could all be eliminated. The net result would
be up to a 30% reduction in fuel consumption. Unfortunately, this is still a dream
because of the inability to produce large, complex-shaped products with few small-
sized flaws. Table 2.1 provides the density of some of today’s advanced ceramics.

to their exceptional hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance. Achieving
these properties requires a relative density exceeding 95% in advanced ceramics.

  Ceramic forming is a mature technology with several traditional methodologies,
for example, pressing, extrusion, slip casting, gel casting, injection molding (IM), and

to the high melting point and low ductility. The very high melting temperature and
low ductility of advanced ceramic materials make processing them from the molten
liquid state extremely challenging, while their poor thermal shock resistance often
results in the formation of cracks and pores when forming parameters and tempera­
ture treatments are not perfectly well-controlled. Traditionally, ceramics are manu­
factured from powder to a green shape, followed by densification or sintering at high
temperatures. Ceramic powders are commonly mixed with a binder and other addi­
tives, such as a deflocculant and a plasticizer, to form a dry powder mix for shaping
the green body by die pressing or cold isostatic pressing (dry forming). Alternatively,
the powder can be dispersed in a liquid carrier to form a colloidal ceramic slurry of
ceramic powder in a solvent for tape casting and slip casting (wet forming) or in wax
for IM (plastic forming) (Yang et al., 2003).
   However, these traditional forming techniques often allow only two-dimensional
design freedom, cannot create internal or multi-scaled features, and require compli­
cated and expensive dies. Pressing and extrusion produce parts of simple geometry
such as disks, rods, and tubes. Slip casting (Le Ferrand, 2021), gel casting (Morissette
et al., 2000), and IM (Wiesner et al., 2014), afford the most geometric freedom but do
not enable material heterogeneity.
   Therefore,  lots of attention has been paid to AM technologies to produce
complex-shaped ceramic components by overcoming their inherent limitations,
such as machinability and formability, by pre-processing raw materials before print­
ing. Figure 2.2 shows a classification of forming techniques for ceramic materials.

2.2.2  Advanced Ceramics from the Perspective of AM

Commonly, ceramic materials can be divided into two main categories: traditional
and advanced (or technical). Traditional ceramics are those made from naturally
occurring materials, such as clay and sand. In contrast, advanced ceramics are typ­
ically synthesized using advanced manufacturing techniques, and examples include
silicon carbide (SiC), silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4), boron nitride (BN), aluminum oxide
(Al 2 O 3), zirconium oxide (ZrO2), composites, and many others. With a precisely
controllable production process for manipulating the composition and, thus, the
microstructure, advanced ceramic materials can have exceptional properties highly
desirable for widespread applications far beyond those of traditional ceramic materi­
als. Therefore, advanced ceramic materials are among the most important materials
demanded in modern industries. For example, the core components of insulators for
hypersonic aircraft, tissue engineering, and micro- and nanoelectromechanical sys­
tems heavily rely on advanced ceramics.
  Advanced ceramics are typically categorized according to their chemical nature
as metal oxides, such as alumina (Al 2 O 3) and zirconia (ZrO2), or non-oxides, such
as carbides, nitrides, or borides (Drouet et  al., 2017). These high-performance
ceramic materials can also be subdivided according to their end-use application into
structural ceramics, electro-ceramics (which include dielectric, piezoelectric, and
pyroelectric performance), opto-ceramics, chemical processing ceramics, ceramic
coatings, bioceramics, and superconductors (Riedel et al., 2008; Frischholz, 2004).
The most investigated oxide ceramics for AM are Al 2 O 3 (due to its versatility, low
price, and relatively low sintering temperature) and ZrO2 (due to its high tough­
ness, relatively low sintering temperature, and widespread industrial applications).
Although silica (SiO 2 ) and silicate ceramics are not always considered to be techni­
cal ceramic materials, they are included in this review because of their widespread
utilization across several research groups as a cost-effective alternative to alumina
and other advanced ceramics in the initial stages of AM research projects or for
biomedical applications. Non-oxide ceramics such as silicon carbide (SiC), tungsten
carbide (WC), boron carbide (B4 C ), silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4), aluminum nitride (AlN),
and zirconium diboride (ZrB2) are usually characterized by a higher temperature
resistance as well as increased strength and fracture toughness.
   Furthermore, while oxide ceramics are relatively easy to process, with sintering
temperatures rarely exceeding about 1550°C, non-oxide ceramics are much more
challenging to process due to their higher hardness, sintering temperatures generally
well more than 1700°C, and the fact that pressure-assisted firing in a controlled inert
atmosphere is often also required.
  While oxide and non-oxide advanced ceramics are typically processed and
shaped according to the powder processing method – that is, shaping and sintering
of a ceramic component from a dry or wet ceramic powder mix – they can also be
obtained from the pyrolysis of preceramic polymers.
   Following the development trend of AM-related research, AM for ceramic mate­
rials has also experienced similar rapid development. Multiple AM methods can
be used to produce ceramic materials, which can be classified based on the type of

feedstock materials or the AM techniques adopted. Based on the type of feedstock
materials, ceramic powder with polymer (i.e., binder) and preceramic polymers (with
or without fillers) are the two most popular materials for AM processes (Wang et al.,
2022). In detail, AM processes with ceramic powder and polymer involve mixing
ceramic powders with binder polymers for the 3D fabrication of solid objects. Once
printed, objects usually undergo a sintering process to remove the polymer and fuse
the ceramic powder, and, finally, the solid ceramic objects are produced (Huang
et  al., 2019). The AM processes with preceramic polymers involve feedstock
materials that usually consist of organic compounds and possess excellent pro­
cessability, which allows them to be easily shaped and molded into desired geomet­
ric structures. After pyrolysis, the AM-fabricated preceramic physical objects will
be further converted into functional ceramic components (Wang et al., 2022). This
kind of AM utilizing preceramic polymers for fabricating ceramic materials can
be grouped into one of the polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) processes. AM
processes using preceramic feedstock materials have been effective and ver­
satile in manufacturing functional advanced ceramic materials with complex
geometric structures. They have been investigated for various applications, espe­
