GmbH in collaboration with Siemens.)

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    303

   b. Support Removal : This is a mechanical post-processing category. Many
      pieces need a support structure to be printed, so before any heat treatment
      or finishing can be affected on the piece, support structures need not be
     removed to help reduce distortion of features on the part; without supports,
      there is a risk of having a build failure if the part warps too much and causes
     an issue. Although a band saw or files might be enough to remove parts and
      support structure, in the case of harder materials that resist intense strain, it
     might be necessary to use CNC machining.
    c. Abrasive Finishing or Grinding: Abrasive finishing and grinding are con­
      ventional manufacturing techniques to improve the form accuracy and sur­
      face finish of advanced ceramic parts in various industries. They are used
      as common post-processing methods for AMC parts because of their high
      maturity and good accessibility.
   d. Mechanical Super-Finishing Post-Processing Operations: The mechan­
       ically based technologies comprise abrasive flow machining (AFM), water
       jet peening (WJP), and oil jet peening (OJP).
       • AFM : This is a purely mechanical process that finishes surfaces and
         edges by extruding a viscous abrasive medium flowing under pressure
         through or across a workpiece. This process provides a high level of
          surface finish and close tolerances with an economically acceptable
           rate of surface generation for a wide range of industrial components.
      A common setup is to position the work part between two opposing
          cylinders, one containing media (visco-elastic polymer) and the other
         empty. The polymer has the consistency of putty. The medium is forced
         under pressures ranging between 0.7 and 20 MPa to flow through the
          part from the first cylinder to the other, and then back again, as many
         times as necessary to achieve the desired material removal and finish.
      AFM is capable of removing electrical discharge machining (EDM),
       EBM, and laser beam machining damaged surfaces and significantly
         improving surface roughness  ( Youssef et  al., 2020 ). For advanced
         ceramic parts, AFM can be a valuable post-processing technique, espe­
           cially for improving surface roughness and achieving a smoother fin­
           ish. However, there are several factors to consider. AFM can access
          internal features, holes, and intricate contours that are hard to reach
         with traditional machining methods. This makes it a good option for
          post-processing advanced ceramic parts with geometrically complex
         shapes or fine features. While AFM can provide a smoother surface, it
         might not achieve the same level of precision as laser-based methods
           (like laser polishing (LP)) in terms of surface smoothness. However, it
         can still improve surface quality to a satisfactory level for many appli­
          cations. The abrasive slurry used in AFM must be carefully selected to
        match the hardness of the ceramic material, as too coarse an abrasive
         could damage the surface.
       •  WJP uses high-pressure water jets to impact a surface, creating local­
          ized surface deformations and compressive stresses. Unlike shot peen­
           ing, WJP does not involve solid media, which might make it less likely

304           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

          to cause cracking in brittle materials like ceramics. The process could
         induce compressive residual stresses, improve surface finish, and reduce
         roughness. Moreover, the absence of solid abrasives minimizes the risk
          of inducing fractures in the ceramic material. WJP could be a more suit­
          able post-processing method for advanced ceramics compared to shot
         peening or cavitation peening, provided that the process parameters are
         optimized to avoid damaging the material.
       •  OJP is similar to WJP, but it uses oil as the medium instead of water.
        The use of oil allows for the lubrication of the surface during peen­
          ing, potentially reducing the risk of damaging the surface compared to
        WJP. OJP offers a gentler alternative to WJP and may be more suitable
          for advanced ceramics, provided that the process is fine-tuned to avoid
          over-stressing the material.

Mechanical  super-finishing  post-processing  operations  not  applicable  for
AMC are:
   Shot peening (SP) involves bombarding the surface of a material with small,
spherical media (shots), typically made of steel or ceramic, at high velocity. This cre­
ates plastic deformation on the material’s surface, which induces compressive resid­
ual stresses that improve fatigue life and surface durability. SP is most commonly
used for metals, where plastic deformation is easily induced. Advanced ceramics,
due to their brittleness, have limited capacity for plastic deformation. This makes SP
more challenging and potentially damaging if not carefully controlled. The energy
of the shots could cause microcracking or surface damage on brittle ceramic parts.
Cavitation peening (CP), which is a process that uses the formation and collapse
of bubbles (cavitation) in a liquid medium to create shock waves that impact the
material’s surface. This process is typically used to improve the fatigue resistance of
metals but has also been considered for ceramics. Ceramics are much more brittle
than metals, so cavitation-induced shock waves could cause microcracks or surface
damage. The high-energy impacts generated by cavitation could be too aggressive
for advanced ceramics, leading to degradation rather than improvement. In conclu­
sion, CP may not be an ideal method for advanced ceramics due to the risk of damage
from shock waves. Its use would require stringent control of parameters like inten­
sity, duration, and fluid type.

10.2.2.1.2  Thermal Methods
These include the following.

10.2.2.1.2.1  Thermal Treatments
Post-processing heat treatment is a common method used to modify the tensile prop­
erties of 3D-printed parts. Heat treatment involves subjecting the printed parts to
controlled temperature conditions for a specific duration, resulting in changes in
the material’s microstructure, crystallinity, and mechanical behavior. The effects of
post-processing heat treatment on the mechanical properties of 3D-printed parts can
vary depending on several factors, such as the material type, printing process, heat
treatment parameters, and part geometry.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    305

    a. Curing: Curing refers to a post-processing step where the printed material
     undergoes a controlled thermal or chemical treatment to improve its final
      properties, such as strength, hardness, and stability. In the case of advanced
      ceramics, curing is typically used to ensure that the material undergoes solidi­
       fication or bonding processes that are essential to achieving the desired ceramic
       characteristics. The curing process can vary depending on the specific AM
      technique, but it is often necessary when the printing process involves mate­
       rials that are not fully solidified during printing or that require additional pro­
      cessing to achieve the desired ceramic properties. Curing is mostly needed for
      processes that use photopolymers, binder-based materials, or ceramic pastes
      (such as SLA, DIW, BJ, and material jetting (MJ)). The main goal of curing
      in these processes is to stabilize the printed parts before they undergo further
      processing steps, like sintering, to achieve the final ceramic properties.
   b. Debinding: It is defined as the removal of binder materials used during the
   AM process. Most advanced ceramics are printed with a binder to hold the
     ceramic powder together. Debinding is the process of removing the binder
      before sintering. It eliminates organic binders and avoids defects during sin­
      tering, ensuring proper part formation and density. While it may involve
      heat, it is not always classified as a full “heat treatment” in the traditional
      sense because it primarily focuses on removing binders rather than altering
      the material’s microstructure or properties. However, it can be considered a
      preliminary heat treatment step in the broader context of powder-based AM
      processes.
        There are two types of debinding, namely, thermal debinding, in which
      the part is heated in a furnace to burn off organic binders without caus­
      ing damage to the ceramic part, and solvent debinding, in which the part is
     immersed in a solvent to remove the binder before further processing.
       The green parts produced by AM usually undergo debinding to remove
      the binder or other organic residue from the printed part. This leaves behind
     a fragile ceramic structure with poor mechanical properties. Debinding is
     followed by sintering at elevated temperatures (up to 2300°C), leading to
      further shrinkage.
    c. Stress Relieving: Stress relieving is considered an important post-process­
      ing operation in AM of advanced ceramics. During the AM process, such as
     BJ or DIW, internal stresses can develop due to factors like thermal gradi­
      ents, cooling rates, and uneven material deposition. These stresses can lead
      to warping, cracking, or failure of the printed part.
         Stress relieving helps to mitigate these internal stresses and improves the
      overall mechanical properties and dimensional stability of the ceramic parts.
        It is typically done through stress relieving, which allows the material to
      gradually relax and reduce residual stresses that have developed during the
      printing or processing phase. The ceramic material is heated to a tempera­
      ture below its sintering temperature, typically between 500°C and 1000°C
      for a specific time interval, allowing the material to gradually relax and
     reduce the internal stresses. The part is then cooled slowly (often by turning
      off the furnace and keeping it cool at a controlled rate).

306           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   d. Sintering: Sintering is a heat treatment process where the ceramic part is
      heated to a temperature below its melting point, causing the ceramic particles
      to bond together, reducing porosity, and enhancing the mechanical properties
      of the material. Sintering mechanisms play a critical role in transforming a
     “green body” (shaped by a multi-step process, unsintered part) into a dense,
     mechanically strong final component. In sintering, the part is heated in a fur­
     nace in the presence of a controlled atmosphere (e.g., air, vacuum, or inert gas)
      for a set period. During this process, particles within the ceramic part diffuse
     and coalesce, increasing density and strength. There are two types of sinter­
      ing, namely, solid-state sintering (SSS) and liquid-phase sintering (LPS).

      1. SSS: involves densification without the formation of a liquid phase. At
        high temperatures (but below the melting point of the primary phase),
        atomic diffusion causes particles to bond and densify. It is characterized
       by the following:
          •  Involves diffusion mechanisms: surface, grain boundary, and lattice
             diffusion.
          •  Grain growth occurs as densification progresses.
          •  Requires high temperatures and long dwell times.
          •  Typically results in good mechanical properties.

       SSS is common in powder-based AM of ceramics like lithography-based
        ceramic manufacturing or BJ, where parts are printed in a loose or bound
       powder form and then sintered. It is also used for materials with high melt­
         ing points and no additives that form liquid phases at sintering temperature.
      2. LPS: is another valuable post-processing step in the AM of advanced
        ceramics, enabling improved densification, mechanical strength, and
          reliability of ceramic components. By introducing a secondary liquid
        phase during the sintering process, ceramic parts printed using AM
         technologies can achieve higher quality, stronger, and more functional
         materials suited for demanding applications in industries like aerospace,
        automotive, and medical devices. In LPS, a liquid phase forms during
          sintering, aiding particle rearrangement and enhancing densification at
        lower temperatures. LPS is characterized by:
          • A liquid forms at the sintering temperature (e.g., from additives or
            impurities).
          •  Capillary forces pull solid particles together.
          •  Enhanced diffusion and mass transport.
          •  Usually faster and can achieve higher final densities.

    LPS is common in ceramic composites, or systems like SiC with sinter­
      ing aids (e.g., Al₂O₃-Y₂O₃). It is used when complete densification is diffi­
      cult with solid-state mechanisms alone. However, it is more prone to grain
     growth and phase changes depending on composition.
    e. Ultrafast High-Temperature Sintering (UHS): In UHS, the part is rap­
      idly sintered (in seconds) by heating up to temperatures as high as 3000°C.
    UHS has been demonstrated to achieve densities greater than 95% while

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    307

      yielding uniform compositions and favorable microstructures for a broad
     range of ceramics that can be difficult to densify with the same results using
      conventional sintering approaches.
     f. Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP): HIP is a thermal post-processing operation
     used to consolidate and densify materials such as metals, ceramics, and
     composite materials. It involves subjecting the material to high temperatures
     and pressure in a gastight container, typically an inert gas such as argon,
      helium, or nitrogen. The material undergoes high-pressure isotropic com­
      pression, which helps eliminate voids or defects in the material. The tem­
      perature used during the process is typically close to the melting point of the
      material, which allows the material to achieve a maximum level of density
     and uniformity. HIP is often used for the production of parts with complex
      geometries that are difficult to produce by other methods such as casting or
      forging, and is used for high-performance materials. It is also used in the
      production of high-performance materials that have high density and uni­
      formity requirements, such as aerospace components and medical implants.
     HIPs are widely used in aerospace, medical, and automotive applications to
     produce high-quality, dense parts with excellent mechanical properties.
         Parts produced by various additive technologies are prone to poros­
       ity due to the layer-by-layer deposition process. This can lead to defects
     such as voids, cracks, and inclusions that can weaken the part and reduce
        its mechanical properties. HIP can be used to reduce porosity and improve
      hardness by applying high temperature and pressure to the part. The high
      pressure forces the gas to diffuse out of the part, while the high temperature
     promotes plastic deformation and defect healing, resulting in a denser and
     more uniform microstructure.
       HIP thermal treatment can improve the mechanical properties of AM
      parts by eliminating or reducing defects such as porosity, inclusions, and
      microcracks. This leads to an increase in strength, ductility, and hardness,
     making the parts more suitable for demanding applications. In addition, HIP
      treatment can be used to improve the surface finish and aesthetics of AM
      parts by applying high temperature and pressure to the part, resulting in
      plastic deformation of surface irregularities and creating a more uniform
      surface. This can make the part more visually appealing and suitable for
      applications requiring a smooth surface finish.
         Parts produced using additive technologies often contain residual stresses
     due to the thermal cycling involved in the printing process. These stresses
     can affect the mechanical properties of the part and lead to deformation or
      failure under stress. HIP treatment can be used to remove residual stresses
     by applying high temperature and pressure to the part, which promotes plas­
       tic deformation and stress reduction.
    g. Difference between Sintering and HIP: While both processes are cru­
       cial in the fabrication of advanced ceramics, HIP is often employed when
      parts require near-perfect densification, such as in high-performance appli­
      cations, while sintering remains the baseline technique for ceramic AM
     manufacturing. The primary goal of sintering is to consolidate the ceramic
      material by promoting particle bonding and reducing porosity, leading to

10.2.2.1.2.2  Thermal Super-Finishing
Thermal-based technologies comprise laser shock peening (LSP) and LP.

   a. LSP: In LSP, a laser beam is used to create a plasma shock wave, which is
      reflected on the surface of the component, inducing a compression residual
      stress (CRS) that deeply penetrates the material, as shown in Figure 10.5.
   A transparent layer is required, although a non-transparent (opaque) layer

Ye, 2006.)


       is also often used. The transparent layer (usually water) is used to reduce
      the plasma produced on the surface and increase the shock wave intensity.
     The temperature at the heating point reaches up to 10,000°C, and the pulse
      length is about 0.15 to 0.30 ns. After the laser beam passes through the
      transparent layer, it hits an opaque layer, usually made of aluminum, zinc, or
      copper, which is also called a sacrificial coating. The opaque layer is used to
      prevent direct laser ablation on the surface. An impulse of laser reaches the
      absorption layer, and then ionization occurs in the heated zone, and a shock
     wave is generated, which plastically deforms the material. LSP is an appro­
      priate method for improving the surface quality and mechanical properties
      of additively manufactured components. Sun (2018) studied the microstruc­
      tural and mechanical properties of wire arc additively manufactured 2319
     aluminum alloy subjected to LSP. LSP was able to impart a maximum CRS
      of 100 MPa up to a depth of 0.75 mm, which significantly improved the
      tensile properties. It significantly improved the microstructure and micro­
      hardness. LSP is widely utilized to improve the fatigue life of compressor
      blades, jet engine fans, and aircraft structures. It has also been applied to
     improve the surface properties of processed maraging steels.
   b. LP: LP is considered a potential method for improving the surface roughness
      of AM parts. It is a noncontact surface finishing process that uses laser irra­
      diation to achieve subsequent surface smoothening, as shown in Figure 10.6
     (Marimuthu et al., 2015). In this process, a laser beam is used to melt the
      surface of the workpiece to reduce the surface roughness. During LP, mor­
     phology apexes can reach the melting temperature. The liquid material redis­
      tributes because of the effect of gravity and surface tension. Once the laser
    beam stops scanning the surface, the temperature of the heat-affected zone
    (HAZ) drops rapidly, resulting in the solidification of the molten pool, and
      the surface roughness reduces accordingly. LP is an automated process that
     changes surface morphology by re-melting without changing or affecting the
     bulk properties.

  During the past 20 years, LP technology has been extensively utilized to post-pro­

by the ability of the re-melted liquid material to be uniformly spread. The formation
of martensite during the re-melting of the titanium alloy resulted in higher hardness.
Reduction in surface roughness also helped to improve the wear resistance of the
components. It was noted that due to LP, the surface roughness was reduced to 80%
than the initial surface roughness (Dadbakhsh et al., 2010; Mai and Lim, 2004).

10.2.2.2  Optional Post-Processing Operations
These are additional steps that can be performed based on the specific needs of the
ceramic part and the desired properties for its final application. They are not always
necessary but may be used to tailor the material’s characteristics.

    1. Infiltration: Infiltration is a process used to fill the pores of a ceramic part
     with another material, such as a metal or polymer, to improve mechanical
      properties like strength or toughness. It has two methods, namely:
       •  Hot Infiltration: The part is heated in a vacuum or controlled atmo­
          sphere, and the infiltrant material is drawn into the part’s pores under
          pressure or by capillary action.
       •  Chemical Infiltration: Using chemical reactions to fill the pores with a
          material that solidifies within the part.
   2. Sealing: Sealing is applied to ceramic materials to prevent absorption of
     moisture or other environmental factors that might degrade their performance

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    311

     and to enhance properties such as surface hardness, wear resistance, and
      aesthetics. It has two methods, namely:
       •  Glazing : Applying a glassy or ceramic glaze to the surface of the part to
          create a protective, sealed layer.
       •  Chemical Sealing: Using a chemical solution to react with the surface
        and form a protective layer.
    3. Coating: To enhance material properties such as wear resistance or chemi­
      cal durability. Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) or Physical Vapor Depo­
       sition (PVD): Thin film coatings can improve wear resistance, oxidation
      resistance, or add other functional properties.
    4. Shrinkage Compensation: Ceramic parts often shrink during sintering, so
     compensating for this shrinkage is crucial in maintaining the final dimen­
      sions. This is done through two methods:
       •  Design Adjustments: The part is designed with compensations for
          shrinkage, typically by scaling up dimensions before printing.
       •  Control of Sintering Parameters: Adjusting sintering parameters such
          as temperature, time, and atmosphere to minimize shrinkage.
    5. Surface Texturing: Etching or other surface modification techniques to
      create specific textures or patterns on the ceramic surface for functional or
      aesthetic purposes.
    6. Assembly and Joining: Joining multiple ceramic parts through methods
      like adhesive bonding or mechanical fastening after printing if the design
      requires assembly.
    7. Quality Control and Inspection: Inspection methods  like computer
     tomography scanning, X-ray inspection, or other non-destructive testing
     methods are used to ensure the integrity and dimensional accuracy of the
     ceramic parts.

10.2.3   Post-Processing Techniques Used in AMC Processes﻿

10.2.3.1   Post-Processing in BJ Technology of Ceramics
The heat treatment performed on ceramics fabricated using binder jetting technology
(BJT) usually consists of a curing process, in which the green body is subjected to a
temperature of around 200°C to strengthen the polymer. Once the curing process is
completed, the sample is transported to a high-temperature furnace. In this furnace,
the printed sample is subjected to a binder burnout stage, during which the polymeric
binder is removed from the sample. After the binder burnout stage, the sample is sub­
ject to a sintering stage under controlled temperatures to allow the objects to achieve
their highest mechanical properties. The density of the final parts is dependent on the
sintering time and temperature. For alumina material, the hardness increased more
than six times when the sintering time was increased from 2 to 16 h. The BJ process
is not limited by any thermal effects, such as layer warping. The roughness and the
porosity of the final objects are relatively higher than those obtained through vat
photopolymerization (VP) processes. To fill the pores, post-processing steps could
involve infiltrating the porous objects with a solution to strengthen the parts. The
surface roughness can be improved by manual operations like sanding or grinding.

312           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

10.2.3.2   Post-Processing in VP of Ceramics
After the fabrication of the green parts, they are subjected to debinding and sinter­
ing, consecutively. The debinding and sintering temperatures depend upon the bind­
ing material and the structural material used, respectively. For alumina and zirconia
materials, the sintering temperature could range up to 1600°C. During debinding and
sintering, it is necessary to sinter the parts under a controlled temperature to reduce
the thermal stresses and avoid cracking. After sintering, the final objects obtained
are highly dense ceramic objects with complex features. The final objects result in
fine surfaces with a low Ra value and minimum porosity, which makes the parts
ready for post-processing operations like grinding, sanding, or infiltrating the pores.
In VP technologies used for ceramics, such as SLA or digital light processing (DLP),
post-processing steps are essential to achieve the desired properties, accuracy, and
surface finish of the printed ceramic parts.

10.2.3.3   Post-Processing in Material Extrusion of Ceramics
In material extrusion (ME), the green parts are formed by depositing the feedstock
material in a semi-molten state through the liquefier’s nozzle while the material is
maintained between a temperature of 200°C and 265°C. Once the green parts are
formed, they are subjected to debinding and sintering processes. The liquid binder
components are first removed by capillary action when set inside the dry alumina
powder at a temperature lower than 200°C. This is followed by heating the parts
over 200°C, such that the remaining residual binder material is removed by evap­
oration and decomposition, leaving porous green parts, followed by sintering the
porous green parts up to a temperature of 1600–1650°C for alumina-based feed­
stock, causing densification and linear shrinkage of the ceramic parts. Ceramics
can be printed with 100% infill density using ME processes, but once the binder is
burned out after sintering, the final workpieces tend to be porous. The porous voids
can be filled using molten metals and form metal–ceramic composite functional
parts.
   Heat treatments to relieve stresses may also be important because residual stresses
readily result in cracking and/or warping of the product. Clean-up of printed parts
can be costly and time-consuming (depending on the AM process and the type of
product). The debinding step, however, can be a primary source of defects and asso­
ciated failures. Sintering of a green-body AM build presents perhaps the most com­
mon challenge for delivering the desired shape and (full) density without introducing
defects and part failures.
  Most recently, a new densification technique called UHS has been reported (Wang
et al., 2020). In this method, the part to be sintered is sandwiched between two car­
bon tapes through which an electric current is passed, providing rapid (in seconds)
heating up to temperatures as high as 3000°C. The process is performed in an inert
atmosphere. UHS has been demonstrated to achieve densities greater than 95% while
yielding uniform compositions and favorable microstructures for a broad range of
ceramics that can be difficult to densify with the same results using conventional
sintering approaches.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    313

10.2.3.4   Post-Processing in MJ of Ceramics
The green bodies formed using MJ processes consist of wax or solvent, which needs
to be removed before the sintering process. The dewaxing is done by various pro­
cesses, such as drying in the dry chamber under a controlled temperature for a cer­
tain time, or putting into carbon black powder that can remove wax through capillary
action. After dewaxing, the objects are sintered at high temperatures based on the
filling material type. The sintering action is generally held for a certain time to burn
the residual wax or any high-molecular-weight surfactant residues, followed by heat­
ing to the maximum temperature of the structure material in consecutive steps. Post
sintering, the objects obtained tend to achieve highly dense ceramic components.
Post-processing steps for ceramic parts produced via MJ technologies play a sig­
nificant role in achieving the desired properties, dimensional accuracy, and surface
finish required for various applications.

10.2.3.5   Post-Processing in PBF of Ceramics
PBF is the process where the powder particles are fused selectively on the powder
bed. The fusing of the powder particles usually happens by focusing laser beams
through a deflection Galvano mirror by scanning each layer according to the sliced
pattern of the 3D model. The successive powder layer thickness can vary from
20 to 200 μm depending upon the particle size. Figure 10.6 represents the layout of
the PBF process.
  The binding mechanism is classified, as previously mentioned, into four types:

    1. Solid-State Sintering (SSS): SSS is a thermal process that fuses the adja­
      cent powder particles at 75% of the melting temperature. Many kinds of
      materials can be processed using SSS. However, preheating of the materials
       is required in this process to increase the diffusion rate of the atoms.
    2. Chemically Induced Binding: In this process, the interaction between the
      laser and the material is very short and avoids the diffusion process, unlike
     what happens in SSS. When the ceramic particle, say SiC , is subjected to
     high temperature, the partial disintegration of Si and C occurs. The free Si
     forms SiO2 due to oxidation and acts as a binder between the SiC particles.
      After the infiltration using Si, a fully densified SiC is formed.
    3. LPS (Partial Melting): This process is for a different binder and structural
      material where mostly metals are used as the binder particles and are smaller
      than the structural material.
   4. Full-State Melting: In this process, the structural material is completely
     melted by the laser beam and fused to form fully dense objects. This pro­
      cess is mainly used for metallic and ceramic materials.

The post-processing steps for ceramic parts produced via PBF technologies play a
crucial role in achieving the desired properties, dimensional accuracy, and surface
finish required for various applications. The selection of these techniques is typically
based on the type of ceramic material used, the intended application of the part, and

314           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

the desired performance characteristics. The fabricated parts are nearly densified in
the SLS process, but the residual binder material can be removed by heat-treating
the specimen. After sintering, the relative density of the parts is increased, and they
are fully densified. Post-processing the green parts by methods such as an infiltra­
tion process, polishing, thermal treatment, and coating can improve their mechanical
strength, surface roughness, and structural integrity, and decrease porosity.

10.2.3.6   Post-Processing in Directed Energy Deposition of Ceramics
Directed energy deposition (DED) is a powder-fed AM process in which energy
(laser, electron beam, or arc) is used to melt material as it is deposited onto a sub­
strate. For advanced ceramics, post-processing is crucial for optimizing material
properties. DED requires thermal treatment to relieve stresses, sintering to densify
the ceramic, and surface finishing via grinding or LP to achieve high-quality sur­
faces. A typical post-processing scheme for DED is given:

    1. Stress Relief Annealing: DED is prone to residual stresses due to rapid
     thermal cycling during deposition, which can result in part deformation
      or cracking. Annealing the part by heating to an intermediate temperature
     (below the sintering temperature) to relieve thermal stresses, then slow
      cooling in a stress relief furnace: after annealing to avoid the introduction
      of new stresses.
   2. Sintering and Densification: DED parts made from ceramics usually have
     low density after deposition, so sintering is necessary to achieve full den­
       sification. Parts are sintered in a furnace at high temperatures in an inert
     atmosphere or vacuum to achieve the desired density, reduce porosity, and
     enhance mechanical properties. To avoid oxidation and contamination, con­
      trolled atmospheres like nitrogen or a vacuum are used.
    3. Machining and Feature Refinement: Parts may require additional machin­
      ing to meet tight tolerances or achieve specific geometries. CNC grinding
     can refine features or remove excess material.
   4. Surface Finishing: DED parts often have a rough surface due to the layer-
      by-layer deposition process, so post-processing is essential for improving
      surface quality. Mechanical or LP can be used.
    5. Coating: To enhance material properties such as wear resistance or chem­
       ical resistance, coatings may be applied to DED-printed ceramics. CVD or
    PVD thin film coatings can improve wear resistance and oxidation resis­
      tance, or add other functional properties.

10.2.3.7   Post-Processing in Laminated Object Manufacturing of Ceramics
Laminated object manufacturing (LOM) is an AM technique where material lay­
ers (such as ceramic powders or composites) are bonded together to form a 3D
part. The process involves sequentially layering material and typically using a
binder material to bond each layer. Post-processing is a critical step that includes
binder removal, sintering, surface finishing, machining, and infiltration to enhance
material properties. Each stage must be carefully controlled to prevent defects and
achieve the desired mechanical, thermal, and aesthetic properties required for the
specific application. Proper quality control ensures that the final ceramic part meets

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    315

the stringent standards for advanced ceramic applications, such as in aerospace,
medical, or electronics industries. The following is the typical post-processing
scheme for LOM:

    1. Binder Removal (Debinding): The binder used in LOM is necessary for
     bonding the ceramic particles but must be removed before sintering to pre­
      vent defects such as cracking, warping, or contamination. Binder removal is
      typically done in a controlled environment to ensure that the ceramic part
     remains intact during this critical stage. There are two Types:
       •  Thermal Debinding: The part is heated in a furnace to, gradually,
        remove the binder material. This process is done in stages, starting at a
        low temperature and gradually increasing to allow the binder to decom­
         pose and evaporate. A common temperature range is 200°C–500°C,
         depending on the binder material. This step may be typically carried out
          in a controlled atmosphere such as an inert gas (e.g., nitrogen or argon)
          or a vacuum to prevent oxidation of the ceramic particles. If necessary,
         a multi-step debinding process might be used to remove organic binders
          gradually without introducing thermal shock. For a slow ramp-up-mode,
         a slow temperature increase (typically 1°C to 5°C per minute) is applied
          to avoid sudden thermal stress that can cause warping or cracking.
       •  Solvent Debinding (if Applicable): In cases where the binder is soluble
          in a particular solvent (e.g., acetone, ethanol), a solvent bath or ultra­
          sonic cleaning system is used to dissolve the binder from the ceramic
           part. The part may be immersed in the solvent for several hours, depend­
         ing on the binder composition.
   2. Sintering: Sintering densifies the ceramic material by heating the part to a
     temperature below its melting point, causing the particles to bond and form
     a dense, strong structure. This is a critical step to develop the mechanical
     and thermal properties of the ceramic. Sintering is performed in two steps:
       •  Pre-Sintering: After binder removal, the part is preheated to a moder­
          ate temperature (typically 400–700°C) to eliminate any residual binder
          traces and to relieve any internal stresses before sintering. This heating
        must be done slowly to prevent cracking.
       •  Main Sintering Cycle: The ceramic part is placed in a high-temperature
         furnace where it undergoes sintering at temperatures typically between
        1200°C and 1700°C. The exact temperature depends on the specific
         ceramic material used (e.g., alumina, zirconia, and silicon carbide). Sin­
          tering is usually performed in an inert or reducing atmosphere (such as
         argon or nitrogen) to avoid oxidation of the ceramic. In some cases, a
        vacuum furnace may be used to eliminate oxygen during sintering. The
          sintering process is carried out in a controlled heating and cooling cycle
          to prevent thermal gradients that could lead to cracking. The material is
         held at the sintering temperature for a specific period, which allows the
         ceramic particles to fuse together. The part is gradually cooled to room
         temperature after sintering. Rapid cooling may induce thermal stresses,
         so the cooling rate is typically slow (1–5°C per minute) to ensure uni­
        form shrinkage and avoid warping.

316           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   3. Final Shaping and Machining : While LOM offers a high degree of
     freedom in part geometry, the final ceramic part may need additional
     machining to meet the exact dimensional tolerances or specific functional
      requirements.
       •  CNC Machining: Ceramic parts are often too brittle to be machined
        by traditional methods (e.g., milling or turning) directly after sintering.
        However, CNC machining is used for finishing operations, especially
       when precise geometry or tight tolerances are required. Diamond tools
          are often used in the machining process, as they provide the hardness
         necessary to cut through advanced ceramics.
       •  Grinding: Precision grinding is typically used to improve the surface
           finish and dimensional accuracy. Grinding is often necessary for applica­
          tions requiring tight tolerances or very smooth surfaces.
       •   Drilling or Tapping : If the ceramic part needs holes or threads, special
           drilling or tapping operations using diamond-coated drills or specialized
         equipment are applied. These methods minimize cracking and damage
          to the ceramic.
   4. Surface Finishing: After sintering, the ceramic part may have rough sur­
      faces due to the additive nature of the LOM process. Surface finishing is
      required to improve the part’s surface quality, accuracy, and performance,
      particularly for functional applications where smooth surfaces or fine details
      are important.
       •   Polishing : After sintering and machining, the part can be polished
         using fine abrasives or diamond-based polishing compounds. This
            is especially important for ceramics that will be used in applications
          requiring high surface smoothness, such as in medical devices or opti­
          cal applications. The part may be polished using mechanical or elec­
         trochemical methods, depending on the material and required surface
           finish.
       •  Grinding and Abrasive Blasting: If the part has significant roughness,
          abrasive grinding may be used to achieve a smoother finish. Abrasive
          blasting with media such as alumina or silicon carbide can be used to
          clean the surface and remove any residual sintering debris.
       •  Chemical Etching: In some cases, chemical etching may be used to
         enhance the surface texture or remove certain surface impurities. This
         can also be useful for revealing microstructural details of the ceramic.
    5. Infiltration (Optional): Infiltration is a post-processing technique in which
     a secondary material (e.g., metal, polymer, or glass) is introduced into the
     ceramic body to improve properties such as toughness, thermal conductiv­
        ity, or electrical conductivity.
       •  Metal Infiltration: For specific applications, the ceramic part may be
           infiltrated with a metal such as copper or silicon. This improves the
           part’s mechanical properties (e.g., toughness, ductility) and can also
         enhance thermal conductivity. Infiltration typically occurs at a lower
          temperature, where the metal melts and fills the pores in the ceramic
           structure.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    317

       •  Glass Infiltration: For certain ceramics, glass infiltration can be used
          to reduce porosity and improve densification. This process can also
         improve the part’s fracture toughness. The part is heated in a furnace
          in the presence of molten glass, which infiltrates the ceramic pores and
          helps to strengthen the part.
    6. Quality Control and Testing: Once the post-processing steps are com­
      pleted, it is essential to perform quality control checks to ensure that the
     ceramic part meets the required standards for its intended application.
       •  Dimensional Inspection : A detailed inspection  is performed using
         techniques like coordinate measuring machines or laser scanning to ver­
           ify that the part matches the desired dimensions and tolerances.
       •  Mechanical Testing: Mechanical properties such as tensile strength,
           flexural strength, hardness, fracture toughness, and wear resistance are
          tested to ensure the part will perform as required in its application. Test­
          ing may involve methods like Vickers hardness testing, three-point bend­
          ing tests, and flexural strength tests.
       •  Microstructural Analysis:  Techniques  such  as  scanning  electron
         microscopy (SEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) are used to examine
          the microstructure of the ceramic part to ensure uniformity, absence of
           defects, and proper densification.
       •   Porosity and Density Measurement: The part’s porosity and bulk den­
           sity are measured to verify that the ceramic has reached the desired level
          of densification during sintering.
       •  Surface Finish Inspection: It can be performed using a profilometer to
          verify that the surface finish meets the required specifications.
    7. Final Inspection and Packaging: The final inspection ensures that the part
       is ready for use or shipment, with no defects and properly protected.
       •  Visual Inspection : A final visual check is performed to ensure that the
          part is free from surface defects, cracks, or other imperfections.
       •  Packaging: Ceramic parts are fragile and need to be packaged carefully.
        Custom foam, bubble wrap, or anti-static materials are used to protect
          the part during transportation. Special packaging may be used for parts
           that need to be transported for further processing or assembly.

10.2.4   Post-Processing Techniques in AMC of Polymer-Derived
         Ceramics﻿

10.2.4.1  Generalized Post-Processing Techniques in AMC of PDCs
As illustrated in the previous chapters, AM of advanced ceramic materials using
PDCs represents a unique and promising approach. PDCs are typically synthesized
from polymer precursors (also called ceramic-forming polymers) that can undergo
pyrolysis to form ceramic materials after the printing process. This offers a pathway
for fabricating complex ceramic shapes that would be difficult to achieve using tra­
ditional (suspension) methods.
   However, post-processing of PDCs in AM processes is a critical aspect for achiev­
ing desired material properties, such as density, mechanical strength, and thermal

318           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

stability. These post-processing steps are typically aimed at optimizing the material
structure and properties, particularly after the printing process, where the green part
(the object right after printing) often has a high polymer content, low density, and is
fragile. Post-processing of PDCs in AM involves several key steps: debinding, pyrol­
ysis, sintering, machining, surface finishing, and possible heat treatments. Each step
plays a crucial role in transforming the green body into a high-performance ceramic
material with optimized mechanical and thermal properties. The precise control of
temperature, atmosphere, and processing time during these stages is essential for pro­
ducing advanced ceramics with high density, low porosity, and excellent structural
integrity.
  The key post-processing techniques in this case include the following:

    1. Debinding (Removal of Polymer Binder)
             After an AM process like FDM or DIW, the green body typically contains
     a significant amount of polymer binder. The removal of the polymer binder
       is essential to avoid defects in the final ceramic structure.
            One or more of the following debinding techniques may be used:
       •  Solvent Debinding: Solvent debinding involves immersing the printed
          part in a solvent that selectively dissolves the polymer binder. Solvents
           like acetone or toluene are commonly used depending on the polymer’s
          chemistry.
       •  Thermal Debinding: This method involves heating the printed part in
         an oven at a controlled rate. The polymer binder gradually decomposes
           at elevated temperatures, leaving behind a porous green ceramic body.
        The temperature and rate of heating must be carefully controlled to avoid
         deformation or cracking.
       •   Supercritical Fluid Debinding: In some cases, supercritical fluids
         (such as supercritical CO2) are used to remove the binder. This tech­
         nique is effective for polymers that are difficult to dissolve using tradi­
           tional solvents.
   2. Pyrolysis (Conversion to Ceramic)﻿
             Pyrolysis is the thermal treatment that converts the polymer-derived pre­
      cursor into a ceramic material. This process involves heating the debound
      part to high temperatures (typically 600°C to 1500°C, depending on the type
      of ceramic) in an inert atmosphere (such as nitrogen or argon). The polymer
      precursor undergoes a chemical transformation, losing volatile components
     and forming a solid ceramic network.
            A slow, controlled heating rate is critical to ensure uniform conversion and
      prevent thermal stresses or cracking. The heating profile typically involves
     an initial ramp-up to a medium temperature (for removing volatiles) and
      then a final ramp to a higher temperature for complete transformation into
      ceramics. The pyrolysis process is often performed in an inert gas atmo­
      sphere (e.g., nitrogen or argon) to prevent oxidation of the ceramic material.
     During pyrolysis, the part typically undergoes significant shrinkage (around
    30–50% in volume), so it’s important to factor in this shrinkage during the
      design phase of the AM process.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    319

    3. Sintering (Densification)
             After pyrolysis, the resulting ceramic part is often porous and needs den­
       sification to achieve the final mechanical and thermal properties. This is
      typically done through sintering, which involves heating the ceramic part to
     a temperature below its melting point to allow the ceramic particles to bond
      together, reducing porosity and increasing density.
             Sintering techniques are performed similarly as previously demonstrated
      in traditional (suspension) AMC, using one or two of the following sintering
      techniques:
       •  Conventional Sintering: The part is heated in a furnace to the appro­
           priate sintering temperature, typically between 1200°C and 1800°C,
         depending on the type of ceramic material. The process can be slow to
         allow for uniform heating and densification.
       •  Pressure-Assisted Sintering (e.g., HIP): In some cases, pressure is
          applied during sintering to achieve near-full densification. HIP involves
          placing the ceramic part in a high-pressure gas environment while heat­
         ing it, which helps to eliminate voids and cracks, resulting in high-den­
            sity, high-strength ceramics.
    4. Machining and Surface Finishing﻿
             After sintering, the ceramic part often requires further machining to meet
     dimensional specifications and improve surface finish. Advanced ceramic
      materials are typically hard and brittle, which makes machining challeng­
      ing but necessary. Depending on the hardness of ceramics and the required
      application, traditional or nontraditional machining techniques can be used:
       •  Grinding and Polishing: Fine grinding and polishing are commonly
         used to achieve a smooth surface finish. This can be particularly important
          for components requiring precise tolerances or improved surface charac­
            teristics (e.g., in applications like aerospace or biomedical devices).
       •  Diamond Tools: Due to the hardness of ceramics, diamond abrasives are
          often used for grinding and polishing.
       • EDM: For very hard ceramics, EDM can be used to create complex
         geometries or precise features.
    5. Surface Coating or Functionalization﻿
             In some cases, surface coatings or functionalization may be applied to the
     ceramic part to improve its performance in specific applications. For exam­
       ple, a protective layer or functional surface treatment can enhance properties
     such as wear resistance, corrosion resistance, or biocompatibility.
             Depending on the application of the ceramic part, one of the following
      coating techniques can be implemented:
       •  CVD: This technique involves depositing a thin layer of material onto
          the surface of the ceramic part via chemical reactions in a gas phase,
        which can improve wear resistance, reduce friction, or provide oxida­
          tion protection.
       •  Sol–Gel Coating: The sol–gel process is often used for creating ceramic
          coatings on ceramic substrates, offering properties such as improved
          hardness, corrosion resistance, or electrical properties.

320           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

   6. Post-Sintering Heat Treatment (Recrystallization or Phase Transformation)﻿
             For some PDCs, especially those that form multiple phases upon sinter­
      ing, post-sintering heat treatment may be required to achieve specific crys­
       talline structures. This step is particularly important for advanced ceramics
      that require specific phase transformations for optimal mechanical or ther­
     mal properties.
             Post-sintering heat treatment techniques comprise annealing, which
      involves heating the ceramic to a specific temperature and holding it there
      to improve crystal structure or relieve stresses from sintering. Certain PDCs
    may require treatments under controlled atmospheres to achieve desired
      properties or prevent unwanted oxidation or reduction.
   7. Characterization and Quality Control﻿
             After post-processing,  it  is important to characterize the ceramic
      parts  to ensure  that they meet  the required  specifications. Several
     techniques are used to assess the properties of the ceramic material,
      including:
       •  SEM: For analyzing the microstructure and surface morphology.
       •  XRD: To identify crystalline phases and assess phase purity.
       •  Density and Porosity Measurements: To ensure that the ceramic has
          the desired porosity and density.
       •  Mechanical Testing: To evaluate properties such as hardness, flexural
          strength, and fracture toughness.


10.2.4.2  Comparison and Challenges of Conventional
          versus PDC Approaches
The post-processing steps for PDCs and Suspension-based AM of advanced ceram­
ics differ significantly in the challenges they pose, primarily due to the nature of the
materials, the processes involved, and the final properties desired in the ceramics.
Here’s a breakdown of the main challenges encountered in each:

    1. Challenges of PDCs: PDCs are typically derived from organic precursors
      that undergo pyrolysis to form ceramics. The key challenges in the post-pro­
      cessing step of PDCs include:
       a.  Pyrolysis-Induced Shrinkage and Cracking: During the conversion
        from polymer to ceramic, there is a significant shrinkage (up to 50%
        volume reduction) as the material undergoes pyrolysis. Managing this
         shrinkage without causing cracks or distortions in the final ceramic is a
         major challenge.
       b.  Temperature  Control  and  Uniformity : PDCs  require  careful
         temperature control during pyrolysis  to ensure uniform heat  dis­
           tribution, preventing thermal gradients that can lead to cracking or
         inhomogeneities.
       c.  Residual Carbon Content: Incomplete pyrolysis can leave residual car­
        bon within the ceramic, which can affect its mechanical, thermal, and
           electrical properties. Achieving complete carbon removal without com­
         promising the structure is challenging.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    321

      d.  Mechanical Properties: The transition from polymer to ceramic might
          introduce defects or porosity, which can affect the final material prop­
            erties. Achieving high-density, high-strength ceramics with minimal
          defects after pyrolysis is a significant hurdle.
    2. Challenges of Suspension-Based AM: Suspension-based AM (e.g., SLA,
     DLP, or inkjet-based printing) uses ceramic slurries or suspensions to print com­
      plex geometries, followed by sintering to convert the green body into a dense
      ceramic. The main challenges in post-processing for this approach include:
       a.  Binder Removal: Most ceramic AM techniques involve the use of a
         binder that holds the green body together during printing. Removing
           this binder (via thermal or chemical methods) without causing distortion
          or cracking is one of the biggest post-processing challenges. Incomplete
         binder removal can lead to residual impurities and reduced mechanical
          properties.
       b.  Sintering Distortion and Shrinkage: Like PDCs, suspension-based
     AM parts experience shrinkage during sintering, but due to the complex­
            ity of the printed structure, non-uniform shrinkage can lead to warping or
         dimensional inaccuracies. The challenge is to optimize sintering condi­
          tions (temperature, time, and atmosphere) to minimize these effects.
       c.  Cracking during Sintering: Ceramic AM parts are typically more frag­
            ile than PDCs due to their green state. The transition from green body
          to fully sintered ceramic can introduce stress, leading to cracking, espe­
           cially for large or intricate geometries.
       d.  Inhomogeneous Density Distribution: Due to the nature of the suspen­
          sion and deposition method, the green bodies from AM processes can
         have density variations. Ensuring uniform densification during sintering
        and reducing porosity is a key challenge.
       e.  Surface Finish : AM ceramics often require additional post-processing
          for surface finishing. Removing support structures, smoothing surfaces,
        and ensuring dimensional accuracy can be labor-intensive and require
          precision.
    3. PDCs versus Conventional Approach﻿
       •  Thermal Sensitivity: PDCs generally require a careful thermal treat­
        ment (pyrolysis) to convert the organic polymer into ceramic, with
          particular attention needed to avoid thermal gradients and cracking.
         Suspension-based AM ceramics, on the other hand, must deal with the
           stresses of binder removal and sintering, where uniformity in shrinkage
        and densification is critical.
       •  Material Property Control: Both methods face challenges with achiev­
          ing high mechanical properties post-processing, but PDCs may strug­
          gle more with residual carbon or incomplete pyrolysis. Suspension AM
         ceramics can have issues with binder removal and porosity, which can
         impact the final properties.
       •  Geometrical Precision: Suspension AM methods post-processing can
         be complex due to issues like cracking during sintering or the need for
          extensive surface finishing. PDCs, being derived from polymers, benefit
        from more straightforward processing post-pyrolysis.

322           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

In conclusion, while both approaches face challenges in terms of shrinkage, crack­
ing, and achieving uniformity, the nature of these challenges differs due to the dis­
tinct processes and material types. PDCs focus more on the control of pyrolysis and
carbon content, while suspension AM focuses on binder removal, shrinkage, and
dimensional accuracy during sintering.


10.3  FUTURE OUTLOOK FOR POST-
     PROCESSING AND CONCLUSION

As a future outlook, there are three viewpoints to be highlighted. These are:

    1. Post-Processing Standardization: Various researchers and scientists have
      carried out efforts to facilitate AM post-processing commercialization.
     Each part produced via an AM process contains multiple defects. These
      defects decrease the life expectancy of a produced part and limit its uti­
       lization. To prescribe a particular post-processing technique for specific
      defects, there is a need to establish standardization of the process. These
      efforts will guarantee a manufactured part’s surface integrity and adequate
     mechanical characteristics, thus avoiding failure during application.
   2. Part Complexity: The post-processing, depending on the complexity of
      the printed features, has some challenges in both cleaning and post-curing
      steps, such as taking out the part from the build plate and removing the
      support structures. In addition, in the cleaning step for removing the excess
      resin between the features, mainly the high-aspect-ratio features are prone
      to being deformed. Thus, printing small-scale features presents more diffi­
      culties in cleaning and removing the leftover resin. Moreover, over-curing
      the parts may cause cracks or breakage of the printed part.
    3. Post-Processing Automation: Post-processing covers a variety of stages
      that 3D printed parts have to undergo before being used for the final pur­
      pose, such as powder removal, stress relief annealing, wire cutting, other
      finishing, HIP, and so on. Some of these procedures still require manual
      operation, wherein skilled operators are necessary for key tasks. It may be
      cost-effective to complete the prototype or even dozens of parts manually,
      but if hundreds or even thousands of parts are produced, the demand for
      post-processing automation in AM becomes extremely urgent. Automated
      solutions for post-processing can improve the overall production efficiency
      of AMC.

In conclusion, AMC is no longer just a prototyping method but has firmly estab­
lished itself as a technology for volume production. However, components made
by AM require extensive post-processing, a challenge that is frequently underes­
timated and not taken seriously. As early as the design phase for a new product,
AM users must take into account and resolve issues regarding suitable, cost-effi­
cient post-processing, including surface refinement. This ensures that the expected

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    323

workpiece characteristics can be achieved. Today, the post-processing of 3D printed
components is still done with costly and highly erratic manual operations, which
make a cost effective, industrial production practically impossible. The right know-
how and suitable equipment are key factors for an economically viable and success­
ful use of AM.
   During AM manufacturing, the post-processing techniques consume almost 43% of
the total time. Reducing the cycle time is one of the significant challenges. Therefore,
there is an urgent need for process automation of post-processing techniques. These
automated solutions can promote production effectiveness. This can be done via
machine or robotic techniques, useful in process automation, process control, and
optimal solutions. To automate these technologies, some companies have also begun
to implement robotic solutions that can install printing substrates, clean powder,
and unload and post-processing parts. Some companies, such as Dye Mansion, are
focused on post-processing machines only. Others, such as Carbon and FormLabs, are
3D printer manufacturers that are adding post-processing systems to work seamlessly
with their printing setups. In addition, some companies, like Stratasys, have intro­
duced new technology like water-soluble supports, Water Works™, which requires
users to simply immerse the prototype in a water-based solution and wash away the
supports, thus eliminating the tediousness of spending several hours removing sup­
ports from newly created prototypes and cleaning them afterward. In conclusion, the
number of advanced automatic post-processing solutions will certainly increase in the
future to adapt to the growing development of the AMT.

10.4  REVIEW QUESTIONS

10.4.1   Solved Questions﻿
    1. What is the significance of post-processing in additive manufacturing
    (AM) techniques from a general perspective?
     Answer: Post-processing in additive manufacturing (AM) is a critical phase
      that ensures the fabricated parts meet functional, dimensional, and mechan­
       ical performance criteria. Despite AM’s capabilities in producing complex
     geometries and reducing lead times, the as-printed parts often exhibit surface
       irregularities, internal defects, residual stresses, and dimensional inaccura­
       cies. Post-processing operations – such as heat treatment, surface finishing,
      support removal, and machining – are therefore necessary to enhance sur­
      face integrity, improve mechanical properties, and ensure conformity with
      application-specific standards.
    2. What methods are used to reduce the stair-stepping effect in AM parts?﻿
     Answer: The stair-stepping  effect, a  result of the layer-wise deposi­
      tion inherent in AM, manifests as visible ridges along sloped surfaces.
     To mitigate this, several strategies are employed. Process-level interven­
      tions include reducing layer thickness (i.e., increasing z-axis resolution)
     and optimizing part orientation during slicing to minimize visible surface
       artifacts. Post-processing techniques such as abrasive finishing, chemical

324           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

     vapor smoothing,  electropolishing,  or  precision CNC machining  are
      applied to further reduce surface roughness and enhance part aesthetics and
      functionality.
   3. How does residual stress in AM parts influence their mechanical prop­
      erties, and what post-processing techniques can alleviate these stresses?
     Answer: Residual stresses are induced in AM parts due to steep thermal
      gradients and rapid solidification during layer deposition. These stresses
     can detrimentally affect mechanical properties by promoting deformation,
      delamination, cracking, or premature failure under service loads. To allevi­
      ate these internal stresses, post-processing techniques such as stress-relief
      annealing, hot isostatic pressing (HIP), and LSP are employed. These meth­
     ods homogenize microstructures and enhance dimensional stability, fatigue
        life, and overall structural integrity.
   4. How does the material choice in AM influence the post-processing
     requirements for a product?
     Answer: Material selection significantly dictates the post-processing route
     due to variations in thermal behavior, chemical resistance, hardness, and
     mechanical response. For example, metal AM parts often require thermal
      post-processing (e.g., annealing, HIP) to enhance mechanical properties
     and relieve internal stresses. Polymers, by contrast, may undergo solvent
     smoothing, UV post-curing, or abrasive finishing to improve surface qual­
        ity. Ceramics require high-temperature sintering to achieve full densifica­
      tion and strength. The material’s intrinsic properties thus govern the type,
       intensity, and sequence of post-processing operations.
   5. What role does the support structure in AM play in the need for post-
      processing?﻿
     Answer: Support structures are integral in AM processes to sustain overhangs
     and complex geometries during fabrication. However, their presence intro­
     duces post-processing challenges, such as surface damage during removal
     and additional finishing requirements. Depending on the material and AM
      process, support removal can involve mechanical detachment, chemical dis­
      solution, or thermal degradation. Subsequent finishing, including grinding or
      polishing, is often necessary to restore surface continuity and dimensional
       fidelity. Optimal support design can significantly reduce the post-processing
      burden.
   6. How does post-processing in AM contribute to the overall sustainability
      of manufacturing processes?﻿
     Answer: Post-processing can enhance the sustainability profile of AM by
     improving part quality and minimizing rework, waste, and resource consump­
       tion. Efficient post-processing enables longer service life of components by
     improving fatigue resistance, corrosion behavior, and wear performance,
      thereby reducing replacement frequency. Additionally, sustainable practices
     such as solvent recycling, energy-efficient thermal treatments, and minimal
      material removal techniques can be incorporated. Advanced post-processing
      technologies also enable the reuse of support and build materials, contribut­
      ing to a closed-loop manufacturing system.

Post-Processing in AMC Processes                                    325

    7. What are the major challenges of post-processing in the additive manu­
      facturing (AM) of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Post-processing of advanced ceramics fabricated via AM is hin­
     dered by several intrinsic challenges. Ceramic materials are inherently
       brittle, making them prone to damage during handling and mechanical fin­
      ishing. Achieving densification often necessitates high-temperature sinter­
      ing, which can induce shrinkage, warping, or microcracking. The removal of
      support structures without damaging intricate geometries is also non-trivial.
      Furthermore, achieving low surface roughness and maintaining dimensional
      tolerances are difficult due to the layer-wise deposition and sintering-in­
     duced distortion.
    8. What types of post-processing techniques are used in the AM of
     advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Post-processing of additively manufactured advanced ceramics
      typically includes:
       •  Thermal Debinding and Sintering: Removes organic binders and
         achieves densification.
       •   Polishing and Grinding: Used to improve surface finish and meet
         dimensional tolerances.
       •  CNC  Machining:  Applied  for  intricate  geometrical  adjustments
           post-sintering.
       •  Chemical Treatments: Involves etching or solvent exposure to enhance
          surface quality or remove residual supports.
             These processes are selected based on the ceramic composition, part
     geometry, and end-use requirements.
    9. How do post-processing techniques in AM of advanced ceramics differ
     from those in traditional ceramic manufacturing?﻿
     Answer: While both AM and traditional ceramic manufacturing share
     core post-processing steps like debinding and sintering, AM introduces
     unique requirements due to the fabrication method. AM parts often exhibit
      anisotropic properties, higher porosity, and more complex geometries,
      necessitating precise support removal and additional surface refinement.
      In contrast, traditional methods benefit from more homogeneous green
     body formation and fewer support structures, thus requiring less inten­
      sive post-processing. Furthermore, AM post-processing often demands
      higher precision in dimensional correction due to layer-induced surface
       irregularities.
  10. What post-processing techniques are used specifically for AM of
     advanced ceramics in binder jetting (BJ)?
     Answer: In BJ of ceramics, post-processing follows a multi-stage approach:
      1.  Curing: The green part is thermally treated to increase mechanical
          strength for handling.
       2.  Debinding:  Organic  binders  are removed  via  controlled  thermal
          processes.
      3.  Sintering: Conducted at high temperatures to achieve full densification
        and desired mechanical properties.

326           AM of Advanced Ceramics and Ceramic Matrix Composites

      4.  Finishing: Grinding and polishing are performed to meet surface and
         dimensional requirements.
             Depending on the application, infiltration with secondary materials may
      also be used to improve mechanical or thermal performance.
  11. How is post-processing handled in Vat Photopolymerization (VP) of
     advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: In VP-based ceramic AM, post-processing begins with  sol­
      vent-based cleaning to remove residual photopolymer resin. The part is
      then subjected to thermal debinding to eliminate organic components, a step
      requiring precise thermal control to prevent crack formation. Sintering fol­
      lows, facilitating particle bonding and densification. Due to the potential for
      shrinkage and deformation, surface finishing – such as precision grinding or
      lapping – is necessary to restore dimensional accuracy and surface integrity.
  12. What challenges are associated with post-processing in material extru­
      sion (ME) and direct ink writing (DIW) of advanced ceramics?﻿
     Answer: Key post-processing challenges in ME and DIW include:
       •  Support Removal: Often difficult due to the fragility of green parts and
        complex geometries.
       •  Debinding and Sintering: Risk of part distortion, cracking, or delamina­
          tion due to thermal mismatch and binder burnout.
       •  Surface Roughness: Inherent to extrusion-based techniques, necessitat­
         ing significant post-sintering finishing.
       •  Dimensional Shrinkage: Requires compensation during design or cor­
          rection post-fabrication.
             Final post-processing typically includes CNC machining, grinding, and
      polishing to achieve functional tolerances and surface specifications.
  13. How does post-processing in powder bed fusion (PBF) of advanced
     ceramics differ from other AM processes?﻿
     Answer: PBF of ceramics requires specialized post-processing due to the
      fine powders and localized thermal gradients involved. The sequence typi­
      cally includes:
       •  Powder Removal: Using mechanical or pneumatic methods to elimi­
          nate loose particles.
       •   Sintering: High-temperature treatment for particle bonding and densification.
       •   Stress Relief: May be necessary to minimize thermally induced stresses.
       •  Surface Finishing: Includes abrasive techniques to reduce surface
         roughness.
            Due to the precision of powder placement and localized energy input,
    PBF demands stringent thermal and mechanical control during post-pro­
      cessing to prevent microstructural defects and dimensional deviations.

11.1  INTRODUCTION

The design for additive manufacturing of ceramics (AMC) considers the process
constraints early in the preliminary design stage. If implemented correctly, it reduces
the iterations a designer needs to undergo before manufacturing, thus saving time
and money. The design aspect is related to any particular feature that can be quan­
tified in the design phase (Figure 11.1). These include the geometric features of the
part’s shape (overhangs, bores, channels, bridging, minimum wall thickness, mini­
mum size, and supports) and process parameters (layer thickness, build orientation)
as presented in Figure 11.2.
  Not every geometry/shape can be manufactured by AM. Each feature must obey
a certain geometrical continuity. If this geometric continuity is not considered, the
resulting part will suffer in its integrity (e.g., deformation, porous mass, reduced
density). The design consideration is any effect on the finished product, including
mechanical properties. The most important design considerations are illustrated in
Figure 11.3. The Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM) objectives include the
following (Alfaify et al., 2020):

    1. Provide tools, techniques, and guidelines for adapting the design with a
      certain set of final manufacturing constraints
   2. Measure and understand the impact of the design process on the manufac­
      turing system to improve product quality
   3. Determine the relationship between design and manufacturing and  its
     impact on designers

11.2.2   Part Consolidation and Assembly﻿

Part consolidation is an important design strategy for reducing the number of parts
and simplifying the product structure to reduce costs and weight and enhance perfor­
mance. It considers the freedom to distribute and configure materials and launches
the possibility of reducing the number of parts.
  The design for assembly reduces the complexity of product structures to obtain an
optimum assembly-based design with minimal processing time, including assembly and
build-up time. The main benefits of part consolidation are as follows (Alfaify et al., 2020):

   •  The complexity of production management and part assembly is reduced.
   •  Tedious assembly operations are avoided.
   •  Assembly tools are no longer needed.


11.2.3   Support Structures﻿

Support structures are required for better quality and accuracy. They depend on AM
processes and/or materials (Alfaify et al., 2020).

  A. In polymer selective laser sintering (SLS) parts, the powder bed acts as a
      self-supporting bed, and support structures are not needed.
  B. In metallic SLS parts, support structures cannot be eliminated.
  C. For powder bed fusion (PBF) processes, the support structure mainly count­
      ers the thermal residual stresses generated during the melting–solidification
      processes.
  D. For metal powder laser-based processes, the large temperature gradients
      generated during the process often require carefully designed, extensive
      support structures.
   E. For material extrusion processes, both thermal residual stresses and gravity
      necessitate the need for support structures.
    F. In metallic AM processes, support structures are often required, even if the
      part is mechanically self-supporting, because supports act as a pathway
      for heat conduction that reduces heat-related failures and thermal residual
       stresses.
  G. Support structures are designed such that designers should consider the
      building time, removability, manner of removal, and quality of the part after
      support structure removal.
  H. The part cannot be printed accurately if the inclination is below 45° with
      respect to the baseplate.
     I. The support structure volume, building time, and manufacturing cost are
      typically functions of the build orientation.


11.2.4   Part Complexity﻿

AM characteristics can produce complex internal features to increase functionality
in various applications. Embedded parts in printed parts allow objects to be embed­
ded in the printed part (Alfaify et al., 2020).

Design for AMC depends on how the material is fed and deposited during the AMC

11.3.1   Design for Liquid Slurry-Based Deposition
        for Advanced Ceramics﻿

Ceramic resin is a photopolymer filled with silica. After printing and firing, the pho­
topolymer network is burned out, leaving the ceramic part. Similar to working with
ceramic paste, the ceramic resin has high malleability and can be used for appli­
cations where the accuracy of the fired component is not critical. These processes
include the following:

    1. Stereolithography (SLA)
   2. Digital light processing (DLP)
   3. Two-photon polymerization (TPP)
    4. Material jetting (MJ)

details and surface finishes. It produces extremely accurate and high-resolution
parts that are capable of being used directly in end-use, low-volume production,
or rapid prototyping. SLA 3D printing is used for custom parts in prototype
